## System 1 — Emissions Data Infrastructure

**Scope:** All modes (air primary, road secondary, ocean tertiary).
**What it requires:** A freight emissions calculation methodology aligned with ISO 14083 or GHG Protocol Category 4, capable of producing tonne-kilometre CO₂ equivalent data by shipment.
**Deadline:** No SDG-mandated deadline. Client-driven demand is already present and will intensify as CSRD reporter deadlines hit (2025–2026 reporting year for large EU undertakings).
**Gap from current baseline:** Analytical inference: workspaces operating without carrier-level emissions factor integration (typically: forwarder receives carrier emissions certificates per shipment, or applies GLEC Framework default factors) cannot produce client-grade Scope 3 data. Gap size depends on current system state; a baseline assessment is the immediate action.

## System 2 — Carrier SDG Alignment Profiling

**Scope:** Air and ocean carriers on all active trade lanes; road carriers in Europe.
**What it requires:** A structured carrier record capturing: SAF purchase commitments, fleet CII rating (ocean), alternative fuel pathway (road), green finance relationships (as proxy for decarbonization pace).
**Deadline:** No SDG-mandated deadline. Commercial pressure from client RFPs referencing SDG 9 and 13 alignment is a near-term trigger.
**Gap from current baseline:** Analytical inference: this is a data collection and structuring task, not a technology deployment. It can be initiated with existing carrier relationship contacts through a structured questionnaire process.

## System 3 — Climate Risk Routing Assessment

**Scope:** Humanitarian cargo and time-critical live events, film & TV, fine art shipments on routes traversing regions with high SDG 13.1 disaster exposure.
**What it requires:** Integration of climate-related hazard mapping into route planning, consistent with SDG 13.1 resilience objectives.
**Deadline:** No SDG-mandated deadline. Operational trigger: FACT: "The number of people affected by disasters surged by more than two thirds, from 1,158 per 100,000 population in the period 2005–2014 to 2,028 in the period 2014–2023." *Source: UN DESA – Goal 13, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal13. This trend is ongoing and relevant to route reliability planning on all three trade lane corridors.

---

This document provides a workspace-anchored intelligence brief on **UN Sustainable Development Goals 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure) and 13 (Climate Action)** as a non-binding international framework with direct operational relevance to freight forwarding operations across air, road, and ocean modes, and to the cargo verticals the workspace serves (live events, fine art, luxury goods, film and TV, high-value automotive, humanitarian).

**Convention notes:**
- The SDGs are a voluntary, non-binding intergovernmental framework. They do not directly impose legal obligations on private-sector operators. All binding compliance obligations in this brief derive from *implementing regulations* (EU ETS, CORSIA, ReFuelEU, IMO CII, EU CSRD, etc.) that are downstream expressions of SDG-aligned policy, not from the SDGs themselves.
- References to SDG targets are cited against official UN DESA source content. Where implementing regulations are named as SDG-linked, those links are labeled as analytical inferences unless a source explicitly draws the connection.
- *Legal Confirmation Required* callouts appear where the workspace's compliance posture under downstream regulations turns on legal interpretation.
- All claims labeled FACT are span-grounded against the source blocks provided.
- All analytical, interpretive, or forward-looking statements carry the mandatory label prefix.
- The workspace is referenced throughout as "the workspace" or by operational role. No company name, individual name, or proprietary product name appears.

**Dates:** Sources draw on UN DESA 2025 SDG Progress Report data, UNECE 2025 data story, and SLOCAT SDG transport mapping..

---

## SDG 9 — Target-by-Target Analysis Relevant to Freight Operations

**Target 9.1** — "Develop quality, reliable, sustainable and resilient infrastructure, including regional and transborder infrastructure, to support economic development and human well-being, with a focus on affordable and equitable access for all." Indicator 9.1.2 is "Passenger and freight volumes, by mode of transport." *Source: UN DESA – Goal 9, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal9.

Analytical inference: Target 9.1 is the SDG anchor for national and multilateral investment in transport infrastructure — port expansion, airport modernization, cross-border corridor development — on the Americas, Europe, and Asia trade lanes the workspace operates. Infrastructure financing tied to SDG 9.1 compliance is material to route reliability for air, road, and ocean modes.

Progress note (FACT): "From 2015 to 2023, global maritime freight volumes in terms of goods loaded grew from 10.3 to 11.6 billion tons, with developing countries' share increasing from 49 to 54 per cent." *Source: UN DESA – Goal 9, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal9.

**Target 9.4** — "By 2030, upgrade infrastructure and retrofit industries to make them sustainable, with increased resource-use efficiency and greater adoption of clean and environmentally sound technologies and industrial processes, with all countries taking action in accordance with their respective capabilities." Indicator: CO₂ emission per unit of value added. *Source: UN DESA – Goal 9, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal9.

Analytical inference: this target is the direct SDG policy hook for aviation SAF mandates (ReFuelEU Aviation), maritime fuel regulations (FuelEU Maritime), and heavy-duty vehicle CO₂ standards — all of which affect the workspace's carrier base and will surface as cost pass-throughs.

Progress note (FACT): "In 2024, global CO2 emissions from fuel combustion and industrial processes reached a record 37.6 gigatons, a 0.8 per cent increase from 2023." *Source: UN DESA – Goal 9, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal9.

**Target 9.5** — Research and development enhancement. Less directly applicable to freight forwarding operations; omitted from detailed analysis under the integrity rule.

## SDG 13 — Target-by-Target Analysis Relevant to Freight Operations

**Target 13.1** — Strengthen resilience and adaptive capacity to climate-related hazards. SLOCAT identifies transport's indirect contribution: "climate change adaptation (Target 13.1)." *Source: SLOCAT – Transport Targets of the SDGs, https://slocat.net/transport-targets-sustainable-development-goals/.

Operational implication: for workspaces handling humanitarian cargo or time-critical live-event and film & TV shipments, Target 13.1-linked disruption data is operationally material. FACT: "The number of people affected by disasters surged by more than two thirds, from 1,158 per 100,000 population in the period 2005–2014 to 2,028 in the period 2014–2023, with an average of 124 million people affected every year over the past decade." *Source: UN DESA – Goal 13, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal13. Route resilience planning for extreme weather events is a direct operational consequence.

**Target 13.2** — Integrate climate change measures into national policies. Indicator: "Total greenhouse gas emissions per year." *Source: UN DESA – Goal 13, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal13. SLOCAT identifies transport's indirect contribution to this target: "climate change mitigation (Target 13.2)." *Source: SLOCAT – Transport Targets of the SDGs, https://slocat.net/transport-targets-sustainable-development-goals/.

Analytical inference: this is the target that makes national-level GHG reporting frameworks — and by extension corporate emissions reporting obligations under CSRD and equivalent national instruments — SDG-aligned. The workspace's Scope 3 freight emissions data, requested by clients reporting under CSRD or equivalent, directly feeds national progress reporting against this indicator.

Progress note (FACT): "2024 likely marked the first year when global temperatures surpassed the 1.5°C threshold, reaching 1.55°C above the pre-industrial level – making it the hottest year in 175 years." *Source: UN DESA – Goal 13, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal13.

**Target 13.a** — $100 billion climate finance mobilization. FACT: "global climate finance flows reached an annual average of $1.3 trillion in the biennium 2021–2022, a 63 per cent increase from 2019 to 2020, driven by higher investment in key mitigation sectors. Sustainable transport saw the largest rise (96 per cent), followed by clean energy (53 per cent) and buildings and infrastructure (41 per cent)." *Source: UN DESA – Goal 13, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal13.

Analytical inference: the 96 per cent rise in sustainable transport climate finance is the most operationally material SDG 13 data point for the workspace. It signals that the capital base for SAF production, green maritime fuel infrastructure, and zero-emission fleet acquisition is expanding rapidly — which has two effects: (a) green surcharges will emerge as carriers service green debt; (b) carrier RFP differentiation on emissions intensity will accelerate as green-financed carriers need to demonstrate utilization of their investment.

## UNECE Regional Transport-SDG Link (GHG Emissions)

FACT: "Road transport consistently accounts for the vast majority of GHG emissions in the UNECE region." *Source: UNECE – Climate and Transport Data Story, https://w3.unece.org/Stories/2025/01/tr_sdg_v3/story4.html.

FACT: "The advancement of SDG 13 (Climate Action) relies heavily on reducing emissions in this sector." *Source: UNECE – Climate and Transport Data Story, https://w3.unece.org/Stories/2025/01/tr_sdg_v3/story4.html.

Analytical inference: for workspaces with significant European road freight operations (secondary mode), the UNECE's identification of road transport as the dominant emissions sector under SDG 13 means that European road fleet CO₂ standards and urban clean air zone policies are the highest-exposure instruments on that mode.

*Note on UNECE inland transport committee source:* The UNECE Transport and Sustainable Development Goals page (https://unece.org/transport/transport-and-sustainable-development-goals) was blocked by Cloudflare during retrieval. No FACT claims are drawn from that source. It is listed in New Sources Identified as a high-priority lead for direct retrieval.

---

## What the Framework Is

The UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015, established 17 Sustainable Development Goals as a shared blueprint for global development to 2030. *Source: UN DESA – The 17 Goals, https://sdgs.un.org/goals.

**SDG 9** is framed as: "Build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialization and foster innovation." It carries 8 targets. *Source: UN DESA – Goal 9, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal9.

**SDG 13** is framed as: "Take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts." It carries 5 targets. *Source: UN DESA – Goal 13, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal13.

*Industry interpretation:* The 2030 Agenda explicitly states: "sustainable transport systems, along with universal access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy services, quality and resilient infrastructure, and other policies that increase productive capacities, would build strong economic foundations for all countries." *Source: SLOCAT – Transport Targets of the SDGs (secondary-tier citation of 2030 Agenda text, tier 4), https://slocat.net/transport-targets-sustainable-development-goals/.

*Industry interpretation:* Transport contributes directly to SDG 9.1 (sustainable infrastructure) and indirectly to SDG 13.1 (climate change adaptation) and SDG 13.2 (climate change mitigation). *Source: SLOCAT – Transport Targets of the SDGs (secondary-tier mapping, tier 4), https://slocat.net/transport-targets-sustainable-development-goals/.

The importance of transport for climate action is recognized under the UNFCCC: "the transport sector will be playing a particularly important role in the achievement of the Paris Agreement, given the fact close to a quarter of energy-related global greenhouse gas emissions come from transport and that these emissions are projected to grow substantially in the years to come." *Source: UN DESA – Sustainable Transport Topic Page, https://sdgs.un.org/topics/sustainable-transport.

## Why It Applies to the Workspace

The SDGs are not directly enforceable against private companies. Operational implication: the workspace is not a regulated party under the SDGs as a framework instrument.

However, the SDGs function as the **policy architecture** from which binding freight-sector regulations are derived:

- SDG 9.4 ("upgrade infrastructure and retrofit industries to make them sustainable, with increased resource-use efficiency and greater adoption of clean and environmentally sound technologies") is the upstream policy rationale for CO₂ intensity targets in aviation (CORSIA, ReFuelEU Aviation SAF mandates) and maritime (IMO CII, EU ETS for shipping). *Source: UN DESA – Goal 9, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal9.
- SDG 13.2 ("integrate climate change measures into national policies, strategies and planning") with its indicator "Total greenhouse gas emissions per year" is the upstream rationale for scope 3 reporting obligations under CSRD, the GHG Protocol, and ISO 14083 freight emissions accounting. *Source: UN DESA – Goal 13, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal13.
- SDG 13.a sets the developed-country target of mobilizing jointly $100 billion annually by 2020 for developing-country climate action. Separately, sustainable transport saw the largest rise (96 per cent) among climate finance sectors in the 2021–2022 biennium versus 2019–2020; the source material does not establish that the $100 billion target caused this transport-sector rise, so no causal link is asserted here. This capital growth is directly reshaping supplier access to SAF financing, green vessel financing, and zero-emission road fleet capital — all of which affect the workspace's carrier base. *Source: UN DESA – Goal 13, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal13.

Operational implication: for workspaces operating across air (primary), road (secondary), and ocean (tertiary) modes on Americas, Europe, and Asia trade lanes, SDGs 9 and 13 are best understood not as compliance frameworks but as the **demand signal and capital allocation signal** that drives carrier investments, client RFP requirements, and national policy trajectories across all operating jurisdictions.

MONITORING — severity: the framework has no enforcement date, but the downstream regulations it anchors are in active enforcement or pre-enforcement windows. Re-check window: ongoing; see Confirmed Regulatory Timeline.

---

## Decided by Source Content

**Q1: Are the SDGs legally binding on private-sector freight operators?**
Decided: No. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development was "adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015" as a Member State commitment. *Source: UN DESA – The 17 Goals, https://sdgs.un.org/goals. The SDGs are a voluntary framework directed at governments, not a regulation imposing obligations on private operators.

**Q2: Does SDG 9.4 directly mandate CO₂ reduction from freight operators?**
Decided: No. SDG 9.4 sets a target for Member States to "upgrade infrastructure and retrofit industries to make them sustainable." The mechanism of private-sector obligation flows through national implementing legislation, not the SDG text itself. *Source: UN DESA – Goal 9, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal9.

**Q3: Does SDG 13.2's GHG indicator apply to the workspace's emissions?**
Decided as framework matter: SDG 13.2's indicator is "Total greenhouse gas emissions per year" at national level. *Source: UN DESA – Goal 13, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal13. National-level reporting does not directly create a reporting obligation for the workspace. The obligation arises through implementing instruments (CSRD, ISSB, GHG Protocol) that use SDG 13.2 as their policy anchor.

**Q4: Is transport a direct SDG contributor or only indirect?**
*Industry interpretation:* Decided: Both. SLOCAT mapping confirms transport contributes directly to SDG 9.1 (sustainable infrastructure) and indirectly to SDG 13.1 (adaptation) and SDG 13.2 (mitigation). (Secondary-tier mapping, tier 4.) *Source: SLOCAT – Transport Targets of the SDGs, https://slocat.net/transport-targets-sustainable-development-goals/.

## Requiring Legal Confirmation

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace's specific downstream obligations under CSRD Scope 3 reporting, CORSIA cost pass-through, or EU ETS aviation surcharges constitute SDG-aligned compliance commitments that can be represented to clients as such in commercial proposals — this is a legal and marketing claims question that requires counsel review.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any jurisdiction in which the workspace operates has enacted domestic SDG-implementing legislation that creates direct reporting or operational obligations on freight forwarders as a class of private-sector operator.

---

The SDGs themselves generate no direct compliance deadlines. All action items below arise from the SDG-downstream regulatory environment the framework activates.

**Item 1 — MONITORING**
Operational implication: the 2030 deadline across both SDG 9 and SDG 13 is the shared horizon for all downstream binding regulations (CORSIA Phase 2 expansion, IMO Net Zero strategy milestones, ReFuelEU Aviation SAF blend ramp, EU ETS full maritime coverage). Workspaces that have not yet mapped their carrier relationships against each instrument's compliance timeline risk being unable to demonstrate SDG 13-aligned emissions performance in client RFPs before those regulations create hard cost pass-throughs.
*Action: initiate a carrier-by-carrier compliance timeline mapping exercise covering CORSIA, EU ETS (aviation and maritime), and ReFuelEU against the workspace's air, road, and ocean carrier base on each active trade lane.*

**Item 2 — COST ALERT**
FACT: "Sustainable transport saw the largest rise (96 per cent)" in climate finance flows reaching an annual average of $1.3 trillion in the biennium 2021–2022, a 63 per cent increase from 2019 to 2020. *Source: UN DESA – Goal 13, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal13.
Operational implication: this capital reallocation is accelerating the commercial availability of SAF, green maritime fuels, and zero-emission road vehicles — and simultaneously creating fuel-cost surcharge pressure as carriers service debt on low-emission fleet investments. The workspace should anticipate green surcharge line items appearing in carrier tariff schedules before they are mandated.
*Action: review standard carrier contract terms now for green fuel surcharge pass-through clauses; ensure RFP templates request carrier SAF/low-emission cost disclosure.*

**Item 3 — COMPETITIVE EDGE**
Analytical inference: clients in the live events, fine art, luxury goods, and film & TV verticals increasingly include SDG 9 and SDG 13 alignment language in supplier due diligence questionnaires. Workspaces that can speak to their carriers' CO₂ intensity reduction trajectories (SDG 9.4 indicator: CO₂ emission per unit of value added) and climate finance alignment will have a conversational advantage in commercial RFPs over competitors who treat SDGs as aspirational background.
*Action: build a one-page SDG 9/13 freight alignment summary for client-facing use, grounded in sourced data from this brief and from carrier-reported Scope 1/3 emissions disclosures.*

---

The SDGs carry no exemptions applicable to private operators, as they impose no direct obligations on private operators. This section addresses edge cases in the downstream implementing landscape where SDG-linked policy may interact unexpectedly with the workspace's operations.

**Edge case 1 — Humanitarian cargo and SDG 13.1 tension:**
Humanitarian cargo operations, by their nature, may be required on routes or under timelines that preclude low-emission mode selection. Analytical inference: SDG 13.1 (resilience to disasters) and SDG 13.2 (GHG mitigation) can create operational tension for humanitarian logistics: responding to a climate disaster may require the most carbon-intensive mode (air) on the shortest timeline. No authoritative guidance resolves this tension in the SDG framework itself. The workspace should document the operational necessity basis for high-emission mode selection on humanitarian missions, as client sustainability reports may need to explain these emissions.

**Edge case 2 — Small island developing states and landlocked developing countries routing:**
FACT: "small island developing States and landlocked developing countries remained marginalized owing to infrastructure and cost barriers" in maritime freight access. *Source: UN DESA – Goal 9, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal9. Operational implication: SDG 9.1-funded infrastructure investment in these regions is a long-cycle variable (10+ years to materially change route options). Workspaces with regular cargo flows to SIDS or LLDCs face persistent infrastructure constraint regardless of SDG alignment ambitions.

## SLOCAT Freight Sector Data Gap — Active Research Signal

*Industry interpretation:* SLOCAT's news feed as of the source retrieval date includes: "The Freight Sector Has a Blind Spot. This New Global Survey Wants to Fix It." *Source: SLOCAT – Transport Targets of the SDGs (secondary-tier, tier 4), https://slocat.net/transport-targets-sustainable-development-goals/.

Analytical inference: this headline indicates that SLOCAT has launched or is publicizing a global survey on freight sector sustainability data gaps. The specific survey methodology, participants, and timeline are not available in the source block provided. MONITORING — this survey, if it produces public data on freight emissions reporting practices, could become a benchmarking tool for the workspace's position relative to industry peers. Re-check window: Q3 2026 (survey publication timeline unconfirmed; estimate based on standard survey-to-publication cycles).

*Specific survey details, participants, and publication date not available from primary sources.*

## UNECE Energy Efficiency in Goods Transport — Positive Trend

FACT: "Despite a continuous increase in goods transport performance over time, the energy consumption per unit of goods transported (measured in tonne-kilometres) is decreasing. This trend indicates that the energy efficiency in the transport of goods is improving." Source context: Germany, 2005–2021 data. *Source: UNECE – Climate and Transport Data Story, https://w3.unece.org/Stories/2025/01/tr_sdg_v3/story4.html.

Analytical inference: this trend supports the case that modal efficiency gains (better load factors, route optimization, vehicle technology) are delivering real SDG 9.4 progress in goods transport, independent of fuel-switching. For the workspace, this means that consolidation decisions (maximizing load factor per shipment) are a verifiable SDG contribution narrative, not just a cost efficiency argument.

## UN Decade of Sustainable Transport Implementation Plan

The Implementation Plan for the UN Decade of Sustainable Transport (2026–2035) was launched on 10 December 2025. *Source: UN DESA – Sustainable Transport Topic Page, https://sdgs.un.org/topics/sustainable-transport. The specific freight-sector workstreams within the Implementation Plan are not available in the source blocks provided.

MONITORING — the Implementation Plan's freight-specific components will shape green corridor investment and modal shift policy across 2026–2030. Re-check window: July 2026 Annual Stocktake. *Source: UN DESA – Sustainable Transport Topic Page, https://sdgs.un.org/topics/sustainable-transport.

The SDGs impose no substantive requirements directly on private operators. This section maps the SDG targets to their most operationally proximate implementing instruments for each of the workspace's primary modes.

## SDG 9.4 / CO₂ Intensity Reduction — Air Mode

SDG 9.4 (indicator: CO₂ emission per unit of value added) is implemented in aviation primarily through CORSIA (Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation) and ReFuelEU Aviation (SAF blend mandates from 2025 onward). These instruments impose obligations on aircraft operators.

Operational implication: for the workspace acting as air freight forwarder or consolidator on international routes, CORSIA and SAF cost pass-throughs are the material financial expression of SDG 9.4 alignment in the air mode. Effect on fine art, luxury goods, live events, and film & TV verticals (which use air as primary mode): fuel surcharge exposure is highest here because these verticals are time-critical and cannot readily shift to lower-emission modes.

*Specific current SAF surcharge rates and carrier-specific pass-through figures not available from primary sources.* The workspace should request current SAF surcharge disclosure from air carriers on each active lane as part of rate negotiations.

## SDG 13.2 / GHG Emissions Reduction — All Modes

SDG 13.2's indicator is national total GHG emissions. Its downstream freight instruments:
- Aviation: CORSIA, EU ETS aviation
- Maritime: IMO CII, EU ETS maritime (in force 2024 for large vessels)
- Road: EU CO₂ standards for heavy-duty vehicles, national urban clean air zone schemes

FACT: "Road transport consistently accounts for the vast majority of GHG emissions in the UNECE region." *Source: UNECE – Climate and Transport Data Story, https://w3.unece.org/Stories/2025/01/tr_sdg_v3/story4.html.

Operational implication: for road-mode operations in Europe (secondary mode), the workspace's carriers are subject to the most regulatory scrutiny under SDG 13's GHG reduction trajectory. Carrier compliance with EU CO₂ fleet standards is a forward-looking supply chain risk.

## SDG 13.a / Climate Finance — Capital Access Implications

FACT: "Sustainable transport saw the largest rise (96 per cent)" in climate finance flows. *Source: UN DESA – Goal 13, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal13.

Operational implication: carriers with access to green finance instruments (ICMA Green Bond Principles, GFANZ-aligned bank facilities) will decarbonize faster and face lower long-run fuel cost exposure than those without. The workspace's carrier selection and preferred partner strategy should weight green finance access as a proxy for future cost trajectory.

## SDG 9.1 / Infrastructure Resilience — Route Risk

FACT: Target 9.1 tracks "Passenger and freight volumes, by mode of transport." The data shows "global maritime freight volumes in terms of goods loaded grew from 10.3 to 11.6 billion tons" from 2015 to 2023, "with developing countries' share increasing from 49 to 54 per cent." *Source: UN DESA – Goal 9, https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal9.

Operational implication: for the workspace's ocean mode (tertiary), growing developing-country share of maritime volumes raises port congestion risk on emerging-market routes. For humanitarian cargo specifically, SDG 9.1's infrastructure gap in landlocked developing countries and small island developing states creates routing constraints that operational planning must anticipate.

---

The SDGs impose no compliance chain on private operators directly. The compliance chain is activated through the implementing instruments the SDGs anchor.

For the workspace's three primary modes:

**Air (primary mode):**
The workspace, acting as freight forwarder and/or importer of record depending on transaction type, sits downstream of airline carriers who are the regulated parties under CORSIA (aircraft operators) and EU ETS aviation (aircraft operators). *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace, acting as a non-vessel/non-aircraft operator intermediary, has direct obligations under any current aviation emissions instrument, or whether its exposure is purely through carrier cost pass-through, requires counsel review per the specific instrument and jurisdiction.

**Road (secondary mode):**
The workspace, acting as freight forwarder or shipper, sits downstream of road fleet operators who are the regulated parties under EU CO₂ standards for heavy-duty vehicles and national clean air zone requirements. Operational implication: the workspace's operational emissions footprint for road freight is a Scope 3 Category 4 (upstream transportation) emission that client CSRD reporters may request as supplier data.

**Ocean (tertiary mode):**
The workspace sits downstream of vessel operators who are the regulated parties under IMO CII ratings and EU ETS maritime coverage from 2024. Operational implication: vessel CII rating degrades at high emissions intensity, which constrains vessel operators' commercial flexibility on certain routes — a supply chain risk for time-sensitive humanitarian or live-event cargo.

Analytical inference: the workspace's most material SDG-linked compliance exposure is indirect — as a Scope 3 emission source in its clients' sustainability reporting chains — rather than as a directly regulated entity under the SDGs or their implementing instruments.

The SDGs generate no direct registration or reporting obligations on private-sector freight operators. Reporting obligations arise from implementing instruments. The following maps SDG-anchored reporting flows to the workspace's operational roles.

## SDG 13.2 → CSRD / ISSB / GHG Protocol (Scope 3)

Analytical inference: the workspace's most proximate reporting obligation under SDG 13.2 is as a Scope 3 emission source in its clients' corporate sustainability reports, where clients are subject to CSRD or equivalent disclosure requirements. Clients subject to CSRD will request freight emissions data (ISO 14083 or GHG Protocol Category 4 methodology) from the workspace as a material Scope 3 input. This is not a legal obligation on the workspace as forwarder, but a commercial obligation arising from client contracts.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any specific client contract clause or tender requirement creates a legally enforceable data-provision obligation on the workspace for Scope 3 freight emissions reporting under CSRD-linked supplier questionnaires requires counsel review of those specific contracts.

## SDG 9.4 → CO₂ Intensity Tracking

Operational implication: workspaces that track CO₂ per tonne-kilometre across their air, road, and ocean freight moves are positioned to demonstrate SDG 9.4 alignment (CO₂ emission per unit of value delivered) in client proposals. Workspaces without this data infrastructure cannot respond credibly to client sustainability RFPs that reference SDG 9 alignment.

*Specific reporting format requirements under any national SDG-implementing legislation not available from primary sources.* This is an active research gap; the workspace should monitor relevant national regulation in EU, US, and key Asia jurisdictions.

Downloads and guidelines The 17 Goals -->   History The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development,  adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015, provides a shared blueprint for peace and prosperity for people and the planet, now and into the future. At its heart are the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which are an urgent call for action by all countries - developed and developing - in a global partnership. They recognize that ending poverty and other deprivations must go hand-in-hand with strategies that improve health and education, reduce inequality, and spur economic growth – all while tackling climate change and working to preserve our oceans and forests. The SDGs build on decades of work by countries and the UN, including the  UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs In June 1992, at the  Earth Summit  in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, more than 178 countries adopted  Agenda 21 , a comprehensive plan of action to build a global partnership for sustainable development to improve human lives and protect the environment. Member States unanimously adopted the Millennium Declaration at the  Millennium Summit  in September 2000 at UN Headquarters in New York. The Summit led to the elaboration of eight  Millennium Development Goals (MDGs)  to reduce extreme poverty by 2015. The Johannesburg Declaration on Sustainable Development and the Plan of Implementation, adopted at the  World Summit on Sustainable Development  in South Africa in 2002, reaffirmed the global community's commitments to poverty eradication and the environment, and built on Agenda 21 and the Millennium Declaration by including more emphasis on multilateral partnerships. At the  United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development (Rio+20)  in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in June 2012, Member States adopted the outcome document  "The Future We Want"  in which they decided, inter alia, to launch a process to develop a set of SDGs to build upon the MDGs and to establish the  UN High-level Political Forum on Sustainable Development . The Rio +20 outcome also contained other measures for implementing sustainable development, including mandates for future programmes of work in development financing, small island developing states and more. In 2013, the General Assembly set up a 30-member  Open Working Group  to develop a proposal on the SDGs. In January 2015, the General Assembly began the negotiation process on the  post-2015 development agenda . The process culminated in the subsequent adoption of the  2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development , with  17 SDGs  at its core, at the  UN Sustainable Development Summit  in September 2015. 2015 was a landmark year for multilateralism and international policy shaping, with the adoption of several major agreements: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction  (March 2015) Addis Ababa Action Agenda on Financing for Development  (July 2015) Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development  with its 17 SDGs was adopted at the  UN Sustainable Development Summit  in New York in September 2015. Paris Agreement on Climate Change  (December 2015) Now, the annual  High-level Political Forum on Sustainable Development  serves as the central UN platform for the follow-up and review of the SDGs. Today, the  Division for Sustainable Development Goals (DSDG)  in the United Nations  Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UNDESA)  provides substantive support and capacity-building for the SDGs and their related thematic issues, including  water ,  energy ,  climate ,  oceans ,  urbanization ,  transport ,  science and technology , the  Global Sustainable Development Report (GSDR) ,  partnerships  and  Small Island Developing States . DSDG plays a key role in the evaluation of UN systemwide implementation of the 2030 Agenda and on advocacy and outreach activities relating to the SDGs. In order to make the 2030 Agenda a reality, broad ownership of the SDGs must translate into a strong commitment by all stakeholders to implement the global goals. DSDG aims to help facilitate this engagement. Info 2025 2024 2023 2022 2021 2020 2019 2018 2017 2016 Since 2015, notable progress has been made in expanding infrastructure, fostering industrial growth and boosting innovation. However, stark regional disparities persist, and many developing countries continue to face systemic barriers to inclusive and sustainable industrialization. To advance Goal 9, countries must boost investment in resilient infrastructure and research and development, expand access to finance for small manufacturers and bridge the digital divide by prioritizing affordable broadband and innovation systems in the world’s most underserved regions. The United Nations is advancing digital inclusion through initiatives such as the Technology Bank for the Least Developed Countries and the Global Digital Compact, which is aimed at closing connectivity gaps, expanding access to innovation and ensuring digital transformation benefits  Target 9.1 - From 2015 to 2023, global maritime freight volumes in terms of goods loaded grew from 10.3 to 11.6 billion tons, with developing countries’ share increasing from 49 to 54 per cent. Asia, led by China, drove this expansion, while small island developing States and landlocked developing countries remained marginalized owing to infrastructure and cost barriers. Target 9.2 - Global manufacturing annual growth rebounded sharply by 9.2 per cent in 2021, stabilized at 2.2 per cent in 2022, then lowered to 1.7 per cent in 2023 owing to geopolitical and economic volatility. Target 9.3 - Worldwide, 31 per cent of small manufacturing enterprises have a loan or credit line, based on available data, but only 18 per cent in sub-Saharan Africa.  Target 9.4 - In 2024, global CO2 emissions from fuel combustion and industrial processes reached a record 37.6 gigatons, a 0.8 per cent increase from 2023. Rising natural gas and coal consumption drove emissions, while record temperatures increased electricity demand for cooling. However, the expansion of clean energy technologies such as solar, wind and nuclear power mitigated what could have been a threefold larger emissions increase. Target 9.5 - Global research and development spending grew at 5.1 per cent annually from 2015 to 2022. The research and development share of global GDP rose from 1.72 to 1.95 per cent in 2022. However, many developing economies saw declines in research and development investment as a proportion of GDP. 90.    From 2015 to 2022, the global number of researchers grew by 4.3 per cent annually, driven by Eastern and South-Eastern Asia. This is reflected in an increase in the number of researchers per million inhabitants from 1,137 to 1,420 globally over that period. Women made up 31.1 per cent of the research workforce. Target 9.b  - Since 2015, the share of medium- and high-tech manufacturing value added has risen modestly, to 44.47 per cent in 2022. Regional disparities persist, with high -tech manufacturing accounting for 48.57 per cent in Europe and North America, but only 16.40 per cent in sub-Saharan Africa.  Target 9.c - In 2024, 5G covered 51 per cent of the global population, with high-income countries at 84 per cent and low-income at 4 per cent. 4G reached 92 per cent worldwide. However, 15 per cent of people in the least developed countries and 14 per cent in landlocked developing countries lack mobile broadband. For more information, please visit:  https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/report/2025/ More details on SDG 9 in 2025: https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/report/2025/Goal-09/ The 2025 Extended Report on SDG 9 can be found here: https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/report/2025/extended-report/Extended-Report-2025_Goal-9.pdf Since 2022, the manufacturing sector has faced stagnation, attributed to geopolitical instability, inflation, logistical challenges, rising energy costs, and a broader global economic slowdown. Globally, manufacturing's share in employment has regressed. While there has been progress in reducing CO2 intensity in manufacturing, it falls short of 2030 target values. To expedite progress towards SDG 9, efforts should prioritize accelerating the green transition, strategically prioritizing sectors, and addressing inequalities in digital and innovation sectors. Target 9.2: o The manufacturing sector rebounded strongly in 2021 post-COVID, but growth has plateaued at around 2.7% since 2022, expected to continue in 2024. Despite this, global manufacturing value added per capita rose by 16% from 2015 to 2023, reaching $1,922 per capita. Regional gaps are stark, with Europe and Northern America hitting a record $4,986 per capita, contrasting with stagnant levels of $163 in sub-Saharan Africa. o Since 2015, global manufacturing employment has fluctuated. Starting at 14.3% in 2015, it dipped to 14.2% in 2020 but saw a marginal recovery in 2021. However, by 2022, it declined to 14.1%, with notable regional disparities. While sub-Saharan Africa and Central and Southern Asia saw slight increases, other regions experienced declines, with Australia and New Zealand recording the highest fall of 0.5 percentage points from 2021 to 2022. These trends highlight the ongoing impact of crises on manufacturing employment growth. Target 9.3: Small enterprises face heightened vulnerability, particularly in low income countries. According to survey data spanning from 2006 to 2023, only 16.9% of small-scale manufacturing industries in sub-Saharan Africa had access to loans or lines of credit, compared to 45.4% in Latin America and the Caribbean. This underscores how global uncertainty hampers investment flow and financial access for small businesses, hindering their resilience and adoption of new technologies. Target 9.4: Globally, CO2 emissions per unit of GDP have steadily declined by 11.5% from 2015 to 2021, with a reduction of 16% observed in the manufacturing sector. Despite these positive trends, global CO2 emissions from fuel combustion hit a record high of 33.6 gigatonnes in 2021, with manufacturing emissions also reaching their highest level since 2014 at 6.1 gigatonnes. These figures highlight the insufficient rate of reduction in CO2 emissions intensity to achieve a significant overall decrease in worldwide CO2 emissions. Target 9.5: After a slowdown in 2020, global research and development (R&D) expenditure appeared to return to pre-pandemic levels in 2021, climbing from 1.72% of GDP in 2015 to 1.93% in 2021. However, many developing economies have R&D expenditure relative to GDP below 1%. Target 9.5: The number of researchers per million inhabitants globally increased from 1,143 in 2015 to 1,352 in 2021, with Europe and Northern America, and Australia and New Zealand employing three times higher than the global level (i.e. 4,050 and 4,696 respectively in 2021). On the other hand, sub-Saharan Africa has been substantially lower, standing at 96 researchers per million inhabitants. Additionally, women remain underrepresented, comprising only 31.5% of all researchers worldwide in 2021. Target 9.b: The gradual upward trend of medium and high-tech manufacturing value added in total value added, rising from 46.3% in 2015 to 46.9% in 2019, was briefly interrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, dropping to 46.8%. Despite uncertainties and economic challenges, the sector displayed resilience with a slight decline of 0.67 percentage points in 2021. In Eastern and South Eastern Asia, this sector accounted for approximately 50.6% of total manufacturing in 2021, whereas in sub-Saharan Africa, it represented just 18.3%. Target 9.c: Mobile broadband (3G or higher) is accessible to 95% of the world's population, up from 78% in 2015. In most developing countries, this type of access is the main way – and often the only way – to connect to the Internet. However, addressing the remaining 5% coverage gap poses challenges. Notably, in Oceania (excluding Australia and New Zealand), the gap remains significant at 31%. Although the gap in sub-Saharan Africa is shrinking, it still stands relatively high at 17%, particularly impacting central and western Africa. climate change reached alarming new levels in 2024, with some impacts already irreversible for centuries. Global temperatures broke records and temporarily exceeded the 1.5°C threshold, highlighting the urgent need to curb greenhouse gas emissions. Extreme weather events – including tropical cyclones, floods and droughts – led to the highest number of new displacements in 16 years, worsening food crises and bringing massive economic losses and social instability. Nonetheless, with bold action, limiting long-term global warming to 1.5°C is still possible. Every fraction of a degree matters in reducing risks, lowering costs and preventing catastrophic and irreversible damage to people and the planet. At the twenty-ninth session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, States set a new collective quantified goal on climate finance and completed guidance to fully operationalize article 6 of the Paris Agreement on carbon markets, along with making additional commitments on mitigation, adaptation and the operationalization of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage.  Target 13.1 - Disaster-related deaths and missing persons dropped from 1.61 per 100,000 population in the period 2005–2014 to 0.79 in the period 2014–2023. Nonetheless, disasters claimed 41,647 lives annually over the past decade. The number of people affected by disasters surged by more than two thirds, from 1,158 per 100,000 population in the period 2005–2014 to 2,028 in the period 2014–2023, with an average of 124 million people affected every year over the past decade. 114.     By 2024, 131 countries reported the adoption and implementation of national disaster risk reduction strategies, up from 57 in 2015. Target 13.2 - 2024 likely marked the first year when global temperatures surpassed the 1.5°C threshold, reaching 1.55°C above the pre-industrial level – making it the hottest year in 175 years. This was driven by rising greenhouse gas emissions, El Niño and other factors. In 2023, atmospheric concentrations of CO₂ levels remained at their highest in more than 2 million years and were 151 per cent above pre-industrial levels.  Target 13.a  - According to the Standing Committee on Finance of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, global climate finance flows reached an annual average of $1.3 trillion in the biennium 2021–2022, a 63 per cent increase from 2019 to 2020, driven by higher investment in key mitigation sectors. Sustainable transport saw the largest rise (96 per cent), followed by clean energy (53 per cent) and buildings and infrastructure (41 per cent). Tracked adaptation finance also rose by 28 per cent to $63 billion annually, mainly through commitments from development finance institutions. Communities around the world are suffering the effects of extreme weather, which is destroying lives and livelihoods on a daily basis. The roadmap to limit the rise in global temperature to 1.5°C and avoid the worst of climate chaos cannot afford any delays, indecision or half measures by the global community. It demands immediate action for drastic reductions in global greenhouse gas emissions in this decade and the achievement of net zero by 2050. However, the absolute number remains high. Between 2013 and 2022, disasters worldwide claimed 42,553 mortalities each year. Further, the number of persons affected by disasters per 100,000 population has increased by over two-third, from 1,169 in 2005-2014 to 1,980 in 2013-2022.  o In 2023, 129 countries reported the adoption and implementation of national disaster risk reduction strategies, increasing from 55 countries in 2015. Among these countries, 122 countries have reported promoting policy coherence and compliance with the SDGs and the Paris Agreement as a key element in the strategy. Target 13.2: The year 2023 broke every single climate indicator and was the warmest year on record according to the World Meteorological Organization. Global temperatures rose to 1.45°C, dangerously close for the first time to the 1.5°C lower limit of the Paris Agreement on climate change. Despite some reduction in greenhouse gas emissions in developed countries, concentrations of greenhouse gases reached record high observed levels in 2022 and real-time data in 2023 show greenhouse gases continuing to increase. Carbon dioxide levels are 150% above pre-industrial levels. Target 13.3: A study in 2023 of more than 530 grade 9 science and social science subject curricula found that 69% contained no reference to climate change and 66% made no mention of sustainability. However, three-quarters of countries reported they have plans to revise their curricula in the next three years to focus more on climate change and sustainability. Target 13.a: Climate finance, reported by Annex I Parties as support provided to developing countries, has increased at a compound rate of 5% from 2015 to 2020, amounting to $41 billion. Although there are a range of estimates and a lack of an agreed accounting methodology on the $100 billion per year goal, the goal was not yet met as of 2021. Without transformative action starting now and within this decade to reduce greenhouse gas emissions deeply and rapidly in all sectors, the 1.5°C target will be at risk and with it the lives of more than 3 billion people. Failure to act leads to intensifying heatwaves, droughts, flooding, wildfires, sea-level rise, and famines. Emissions should already be decreasing now and will need to be cut almost by half by 2030 - a mere seven years from now. To combat climate change and its impacts by 2030, urgent and transformative action is needed to meet the commitments under the Paris Agreement across mitigation and adaptation efforts. Target 13.1: The number of deaths and missing persons due to disasters per 100,000 population has steadily decreased from 1.64 during 2005-2015 to 0.86 during 2012-2021. Additionally, 70% of young people can only describe the broad principles of climate change in 2022. Climate finance remains primarily targeted to mitigation; however, and adaptation finance continues to lag, with international finance flows to developing countries 5-10 times below estimated needs. Description Publications Events Documents Statements Milestones Description The role of transport in sustainable development was first recognized at the 1992 United Nation’s Earth Summit and reinforced in its outcome document – Agenda 21. In undertaking the five-year review of the implementation of Agenda 21 during its nineteenth Special Session in 1997, the UN General Assembly further noted that, over the next twenty years, transportation would be expected to be the major driving force behind a growing world demand for energy (Indeed, it is now the largest end-use of energy in developed countries and the fastest growing one in most developing countries). Further, at the 2002 World Summit on Sustainable Development, the role of transport was once again captured in the outcome document - the Johannesburg Plan of Implementation (JPOI). JPOI provided multiple anchor points for sustainable transport, in the context of infrastructure, public transport systems, goods delivery networks, affordability, efficiency and convenience of transportation, as well as improving urban air quality and health, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The global attention to transport has continued in recent years. World leaders recognized unanimously at the 2012 United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development (Rio +20) that transportation and mobility are central to sustainable development. Sustainable transportation can enhance economic growth and improve accessibility. Sustainable transport achieves better integration of the economy while respecting the environment. improving social equity, health, resilience of cities, urban-rural linkages and productivity of rural areas Subsequently, the UN Secretary-General, as part of his Five-Year Action Agenda, identified transport as a major component of sustainable development. To this end, the Secretary General established and launched in August 2014 a High Level Advisory Group on Sustainable Transport (HLAG-ST), representing all modes of transport including road, rail, aviation, marine, ferry, and urban public transport providers. The policy recommendations of the Advisory Group were submitted to the Secretary-General in a global sustainable transport outlook report, entitled "Mobilizing Sustainable Transport for Development", released at the first Global Sustainable Transport Conference in November 2016. The importance of sustainable transport for countries in special situations is also recognized by the international community, through the Istanbul Programme of Action for the LDCs, the Vienna Programme of Action for the LLDCs, the SAMOA Pathway for SIDS, the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, and the New Urban Agenda. In the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, sustainable transport is mainstreamed across several SDGs and targets, especially those related to food security, health, energy, economic growth, infrastructure, and cities and human settlements. The importance of transport for climate action is further recognized under the UNFCCC - the transport sector will be playing a particularly important role in the achievement of the Paris Agreement, given the fact close to a quarter of energy-related global greenhouse gas emissions come from transport and that these emissions are projected to grow substantially in the years to come. The advancement of SDG 13 (Climate Action) relies heavily on reducing emissions in this sector. R oad transport consistently accounts for the vast majority of GHG emissions in the UNECE region, as shown in Figure 1, which captures data over the past three decades. R ail transport , though a much smaller contributor to GHG emissions, has remained relatively stable over this period. Rail offers a more energy-efficient and lower-emission alternative for both passenger and freight transport. Shipping , covering all water-borne transport including inland waterway and maritime transport, contributes only a minor share of total emissions. A sharp decline in emissions was observed in 2020, coinciding with the global COVID-19 pandemic. The rebound seen in 2021 and beyond reflects a partial recovery in transport activity, though emissions levels remain below their pre-pandemic peak. Figure 1 Inland transport GHG emissions in UNECE region, 1990-2023 Source: EDGAR - The Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research . Figures pertain to 49 UNECE countries with available data. Rail emissions data include railways, pipelines, and off-road transport. Shipping emissions data include both inland waterway and maritime transport (following the classification system used by the IPCC). Zero-Emission Passenger Cars As highlighted in the previous section, road transport is the largest contributor to GHG emissions in the UNECE region, with CO 2 making up the vast majority of these emissions. Transitioning to zero-emission vehicles is critical to meeting climate goals and reducing the sector’s environmental impact. Tracking new registrations of passenger cars by fuel type provides valuable insights into the carbon intensity of the vehicle fleet in the years to come. This data supports SDG 13 by monitoring the transition from fossil fuel dependence to more sustainable energy sources in the transport sector. Policymakers and stakeholders can assess the effectiveness of emission-reduction initiatives by monitoring the uptake of zero-emission passenger cars. These insights also help shape policies and infrastructure development to facilitate the adoption of clean-energy vehicles. The UNECE region has witnessed a sharp increase in new electric passenger car registrations over the past decade. Germany has emerged as a frontrunner in this movement, with over 450,000 new electric vehicle (EV) registrations in 2022 alone. However, when it comes to the proportion of EVs within the total passenger car fleet, Norway leads the way. Known for its aggressive and long-standing EV policies, Norway boasts a remarkable 20% of its passenger car fleet being electric, solidifying its position as a global leader in the transition to electric mobility. Several other UNECE countries have also made significant strides in EV adoption. Yet, despite these advances, the proportion of EVs in the total passenger car fleets across most UNECE countries remains relatively small. Outside of Norway, the vast majority of UNECE countries (with available data) have less than 5% of their fleets made up of electric vehicles. In particular, countries like Türkiye , Cyprus , and Poland currently have low proportions of EVs, underscoring the ongoing challenge of achieving widespread adoption across the region. Figure 2 Proportion of electric passenger cars in the total fleet of passenger cars, 2022 Source: UNECE Transport Statistics Database Technology Improvements and Their Impact on Vehicle Emissions The weight of new vehicles significantly affects their CO₂ emissions. Heavier cars generally require more energy for propulsion, leading to higher emissions. However, this relationship is evolving, particularly with the rise of electric vehicles, whose batteries contribute substantial weight but result in low er CO 2 emissions. Data from the years 20 13 and 20 22 across selected European countries show a trend of decreasing CO 2 emissions despite an increase in vehicle weight. This can be attributed to several factors , including the weight of batteries in electric vehicles and overall improvement s in the fuel efficiency in newer vehicle models .    Figure 3 New passenger car average weight against new passenger car average CO 2 emissions Source: Eurostat Database Technological improvements have also played a significant role in reducing energy consumption and, consequently, CO2 emissions in Germany. Despite a continuous increase in goods transport performance over time, the energy consumption per unit of goods transported (measured in tonne-kilometres) is decreasing. This trend indicates that the energy efficiency in the transport of goods is improving. All News Partners Contact Us Transport Targets of Sustainable Development Goals The 2030 Agenda states that “sustainable transport systems, along with universal access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy services, quality and resilient infrastructure, and other policies that increase productive capacities, would build strong economic foundations for all countries” (para 27). The text includes five targets that are directly related to the transport sector and seven other targets that are indirectly related to the transport sector. Transport contributes directly to five targets on road safety (Target 3.6); energy efficiency (Target 7.3); sustainable infrastructure (Target 9.1), urban access (Target 11.2), and fossil fuel subsidies (Target 12.c) emphasize that sustainable transport is not needed solely for its own sake, but rather is essential to facilitate the achievement of a wide variety of SDGs: Transport also contributes indirectly to seven SDG targets on agricultural productivity (Target 2.3), air pollution (Target 3.9), access to safe drinking water (Target 6.1), sustainable cities (Target 11.6), reduction of food loss (Target 12.3), climate change adaptation (Target 13.1), and climate change mitigation (Target 13.2): For more information on SDGs and transport, please go to here . ## Effective Date and Deadline (Required Slots)

**[effective_date]** The Directive was done at Brussels, 28 March 1983. *Source: Council Directive 83/127/EEC, closing clause, EUR-Lex CELEX:31983L0127*

**[primary_deadline]** With effect from 1 July 1984 at the latest, Member States shall admit duty-free a quantity of 200 litres of motor fuel, per the amended Article 3(1) of Directive 68/297/EEC. *Source: Council Directive 83/127/EEC, Article 1, EUR-Lex CELEX:31983L0127*

This brief covers Council Directive 83/127/EEC of 28 March 1983 amending Directive 68/297/EEC on the standardization of provisions regarding the duty-free admission of fuel contained in the fuel tanks of commercial motor vehicles (CELEX 31983L0127, OJ L 91, 9.4.1983).

The brief is structured as a Regulatory Fact Document. Sections without grounded content from the source corpus are labeled as a gap rather than filled in. All claims are labelled FACT, ANALYSIS, or GAP per the provenance contract.

**Coverage note:** This authoring pass reviewed the Directive's own recitals, Articles 1-2, and EUR-Lex ELI metadata as captured; it does not independently review the current consolidated text of Directive 68/297/EEC or confirm whether either instrument remains practically applied following the 1993 completion of the EU internal market, both are labeled gaps rather than assumed.

## Enforcement and Penalty Position (Required Slot)

**[penalty_summary]** *Gap:* the Directive text reviewed in this authoring pass amends the duty-free fuel quantity threshold in Directive 68/297/EEC but does not itself prescribe a penalty, fine, or sanctions regime applicable to Member States or traders for non-compliance; any such regime would sit in national implementing measures, which have not been reviewed in this pass.

## Addressee and Why This Applies to the Workspace

**[jurisdictional_scope]** This Directive is addressed to the Member States. *Source: Council Directive 83/127/EEC, Article 2, EUR-Lex CELEX:31983L0127*

*Operational implication:* the 200-litre duty-free fuel-tank threshold set by this Directive applied to commercial motor vehicles crossing internal Community frontiers under the pre-1993 internal-border customs regime; whether this threshold is still cited or applied in practice following the 1993 completion of the EU internal market and removal of routine internal frontier customs controls has not been confirmed in this authoring pass.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether Directive 68/297/EEC (as amended by this Directive) remains formally in force and practically applied today, and the pre-amendment duty-free fuel quantity that Article 3(1) replaced, have not been confirmed in this authoring pass. EUR-Lex ELI metadata for this instrument records it as in force as of the capture date, which is a formal-status indicator only, not confirmation of current operational relevance.

## What the Directive Does

Directive 68/297/EEC laid down the minimum quantity of fuel contained in the fuel tanks of commercial motor vehicles which must be admitted duty-free at the internal frontiers of the Community; the said quantity, in order to facilitate passage at these frontiers, is increased by this Directive. *Source: Council Directive 83/127/EEC, recitals, EUR-Lex CELEX:31983L0127*

**[operative_amendment]** In Article 3 of Directive 68/297/EEC, paragraph 1 shall be replaced: with effect from 1 July 1984 at the latest, Member States shall admit duty-free a quantity of 200 litres of motor fuel. *Source: Council Directive 83/127/EEC, Article 1, EUR-Lex CELEX:31983L0127*

## Enforcement and Penalty Position (Required Slot)

**[penalty_summary]** *Gap:* no penalty: the source presents this as a Commission Recommendation, a non-binding EU instrument under (former) Article 249 EC, and the text reviewed in this authoring pass contains no penalty, fine, or sanctions mechanism -- Member States are invited to "consider" and "should" act, not required to.

This brief covers the Commission Recommendation of 8 May 2006 on the promotion of shore-side electricity for use by ships at berth in Community ports (2006/339/EC, CELEX 32006H0339, Text with EEA relevance).

The brief is structured as a Regulatory Fact Document. Sections without grounded content from the source corpus are labeled as a gap rather than filled in. All claims are labelled FACT, ANALYSIS, or GAP per the provenance contract.

**Coverage note:** This authoring pass reviewed the Recommendation's legal-basis recital, the seven numbered recommendations, and the closing clause. The Annex referenced in recommendation 2 (cost-effectiveness and practicality advice) was not transcribed in this pass.

## Closing Clause and Why This Applies to the Workspace

Done at Brussels, 8 May 2006. *Source: Commission Recommendation 2006/339/EC, closing clause, EUR-Lex CELEX:32006H0339*

*Operational implication:* although non-binding, this Recommendation is an early EU policy signal on shore power / cold ironing as a port air-quality and noise measure; it foreshadows later binding EU shore-power requirements for ports and ships (e.g. under subsequent alternative-fuels-infrastructure and maritime-emissions legislation, not reviewed in this pass) and is useful background for ocean-freight sustainability and port-call planning.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any later binding EU shore-power mandate has since superseded or built upon this 2006 Recommendation has not been confirmed in this authoring pass.

## What the Recommendation Does

Adopted by the Commission of the European Communities having regard to the Treaty establishing the European Community, and in particular Article 211 thereof. *Source: Commission Recommendation 2006/339/EC, preamble, EUR-Lex CELEX:32006H0339*

**Recommendation 1:** Member States should consider the installation of shore-side electricity for use by ships at berth in ports; particularly in ports where air quality limit values are exceeded or where public concern is expressed about high levels of noise nuisance, and especially in berths situated near residential areas. *Source: Commission Recommendation 2006/339/EC, point 1, EUR-Lex CELEX:32006H0339*

**Recommendation 7:** Member States should report to the Commission on the action they intend to take to reduce ship emissions in ports, particularly where air quality limit values are exceeded. *Source: Commission Recommendation 2006/339/EC, point 7, EUR-Lex CELEX:32006H0339*

## Effective Date and Deadline (Required Slots)

**[effective_date]** *Gap:* the source presents this as a Recommendation adopted under (former) Article 211 EC -- an EU instrument category that Article 249 EC states "shall have no binding force" -- done at Brussels on 8 May 2006, its adoption date; the captured text contains no separate entry-into-force article, consistent with the Recommendation's non-binding, self-executing character.

**[jurisdictional_scope]** The Recommendation is addressed to Member States regarding shore-side electricity for ships at berth in Community ports, with particular emphasis on ports where air quality limit values are exceeded, near residential areas, or where noise-nuisance concerns are raised. *Source: Commission Recommendation 2006/339/EC, point 1, EUR-Lex CELEX:32006H0339*

**[primary_deadline]** *Gap:* the source presents this as a voluntary Recommendation with no mandated compliance date as of 8 May 2006; the text reviewed in this authoring pass sets no deadline for any of the seven recommended actions.

## A. GHG Emissions Coverage for Offshore Ships (new Part AA of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2015/757)

FACT: The new Part AA defines the spatial scope of coverage as follows: "Greenhouse gas emissions from offshore ships shall cover greenhouse gas emissions released during voyages from last port of call to a port of call under the jurisdiction of a Member State and from a port of call under the jurisdiction of a Member State to next port of call, as well as within ports of call under the jurisdiction of a Member State." *Source: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/3214, European Commission, 16 October 2024. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R3214

**Qualification — icebreaker carve-out:** The coverage applies to the enumerated ship types "other than icebreakers." *Source: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/3214, European Commission, 16 October 2024. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R3214

**Qualification — design/certification condition:** Coverage applies only to ships "designed or certified to perform service activities offshore or at offshore installations." *Source: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/3214, European Commission, 16 October 2024. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R3214

## C. Zero-Rating of Sustainable Fuels (amended Part C, point 1.2., Annex II)

FACT: The amended Annex II provision reads: "By way of derogation from point 1.1, companies shall not apply the rules laid down in Part A of Annex I to this Regulation as regards the determination of the CO₂ emission factors where the company uses Renewable Fuels of Non-Biological Origin (RFNBO), Recycled Carbon Fuel (RCF) or synthetic low-carbon fuel. **Rationale stated in the regulation:**

FACT: "Maritime transport greenhouse gas emissions are included in the EU ETS since the reporting period starting on 1 January 2024. ## 1. Per-Voyage Monitoring Infrastructure

**Scope:** All offshore vessels under the workspace's MRV responsibility that call at EEA Member State ports.
**Deadline:** From 1 January 2025 (monitoring must have commenced; the first verified report is due 31 March 2026).
**Gap from current baseline:** *Operational implication:* Workspaces that have not previously operated within the MRV system face a complete build — vessel-level fuel consumption tracking, CO₂/CH₄/N₂O emission calculation, per-voyage event logging (departure, arrival, port call start/end, crew relief events), and integration with THETIS-MRV. The EC's own study found that "the majority of companies managing smaller vessels would need to set up and familiarise themselves with MRV processes as they are not already reporting under MRV." *Source: European Commission – Report COM(2025) 109 final, European Commission, 18 March 2025. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025DC0109

FACT: Estimated annual recurring MRV administrative cost per vessel (for smaller vessels entering the MRV scope) was found to be "EUR 3 690 per vessel on average" in the Commission's supporting study. *Source: European Commission – Report COM(2025) 109 final, European Commission, 18 March 2025. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025DC0109

## 2. Verified Monitoring Plan

**Scope:** Each offshore ship individually.
**Deadline:** Within three months of first EEA port call from 1 January 2025.
**Gap from current baseline:** *Operational implication:* The monitoring plan must be assessed by an accredited verifier before submission to the administering authority — this is a prerequisite step, not a concurrent one, and adds lead time.

## 3. CO₂ Emission Factor Update for RFNBO/RCF/Synthetic Low-Carbon Fuel Users

**Scope:** Any vessel that has consumed RFNBO, RCF, or synthetic low-carbon fuel since 1 January 2024.
**Deadline:** Retroactive to 1 January 2024; must be reflected in 2024 reporting year emissions reports.
**Gap from current baseline:** *Operational implication:* Workspaces whose managed vessels consumed any of these fuel types in 2024 should verify that their MRV reporting system applies the Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/2066 methodology rather than the Annex I default CO₂ emission factors. The original Annex I factors would have produced incorrect (overstated) emission figures and potentially incorrect ETS surrender calculations.

## 4. THETIS-MRV Account and Administering Authority Attribution

**Scope:** All companies newly entering MRV scope for offshore ships.
**Deadline:** Before monitoring plan submission (immediate).
**Gap from current baseline:** *Operational implication:* THETIS-MRV onboarding includes requesting attribution to an administering authority. Only 3% of shipowners managing smaller vessels were already registered in THETIS-MRV as of October 2024, indicating a significant registration backlog among the newly in-scope population. *Source: European Commission – Report COM(2025) 109 final, European Commission, 18 March 2025. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025DC0109

## 5. ETS Allowance Infrastructure (for vessels ≥5,000 GT) — Planning Phase Now

**Scope:** Offshore ships of 5,000 GT and above.
**Deadline:** Maritime Operator Holding Account and allowance surrender infrastructure required before 1 January 2027 (ETS inclusion); first surrender deadline for 2027 emissions falls in 2028.
**Gap from current baseline:** *Operational implication:* Workspaces that have not previously surrendered EU ETS allowances for maritime operations must open a Maritime Operator Holding Account in the Union Registry, which involves a separate registration process from THETIS-MRV. Given that offshore ships only enter ETS scope in 2027, planning should begin now.

FACT: For offshore vessels specifically in the 400–4,999 GT segment, the report found total CO₂ emissions of 3.41 MtCO₂, representing 2.7% of total MRV-covered CO₂ emissions in 2023. There were 921 such vessels. *Source: European Commission – Report COM(2025) 109 final, European Commission, 18 March 2025. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025DC0109

FACT: The report found that "the ratio between administrative costs and coverage of GHG emissions would be on average seven times higher for smaller vessels, compared to the larger vessels already reporting under MRV." *Source: European Commission – Report COM(2025) 109 final, European Commission, 18 March 2025. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025DC0109

*Analytical inference:* The economic case for extending ETS to small offshore vessels (400–4,999 GT) is marginal on a standalone MRV basis, but the Commission has explicitly reserved the question for the 2026 ETS Directive review. Workspaces with a fleet concentrated below 5,000 GT should treat the 2026 review as a material planning horizon.

## FuelEU Maritime Regulation — Operational Intersection

FACT: The EMSA MRV page confirms: "All monitored and recorded data under the MRV maritime Regulation can indeed be used for FuelEU calculations, subject to confirmation by FuelEU Verifier, if different from the MRV Verifier." The FuelEU Maritime Regulation entered into application in 2025. *Source: European Commission – Report COM(2025) 109 final, European Commission, 18 March 2025. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025DC0109

*Operational implication:* For workspaces operating or chartering vessels on EU routes, the MRV data collected under Regulation (EU) 2015/757 (as amended by 2024/3214) feeds directly into FuelEU Maritime compliance calculation. Investment in high-quality MRV monitoring infrastructure serves a dual compliance purpose from 2025 onward.

---

## Icebreaker Exclusion

FACT: The enumerated offshore ship type coverage explicitly excludes icebreakers: the list applies to ships "other than icebreakers, designed or certified to perform service activities offshore or at offshore installations." *Source: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/3214, European Commission, 16 October 2024. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R3214

## Ships Operated in Stationary Mode

FACT: Per ABS (citing EC guidance): ships operated in stationary mode (e.g., FPSOs producing electricity or heating while moored) are covered by the EU ETS for stationary installations rather than maritime transport when operating in stationary mode. "Such ships will not be subject to other obligations as set in the MRV Maritime Regulation, such as reporting emissions within a port of call, as long as they remain stationary." *Source: ABS Regulatory News No. 02/2025 – Application of EU MRV and EU ETS to Offshore Ships, American Bureau of Shipping, February 2025. https://ww2.eagle.org/content/dam/eagle/regulatory-news/2025/Application-of-EU-MRV-and-EU-ETS-to-Offshore-Ships.pdf

## Standard MRV Exempted Categories

FACT: Per the Commission's MRV review report: "MRV exempted categories are defined in Article 2(2) of the MRV maritime Regulation; those are 'warships, naval auxiliaries, fish-catching or fish-processing ships, wooden ships of a primitive build, ships not propelled by mechanical means, or government ships used for non-commercial purposes'." *Source: European Commission – Report COM(2025) 109 final, European Commission, 18 March 2025. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025DC0109

## Offshore Ships 400–4,999 GT — ETS Exemption (for now)

FACT: Per ABS: "A company that is only responsible for offshore vessels (and not responsible for other ship types) does not need to open a Maritime Operator Holding Account, as the EU ETS does not apply to these ships before 2027." *Source: ABS Regulatory News No. 02/2025 – Application of EU MRV and EU ETS to Offshore Ships, American Bureau of Shipping, February 2025. https://ww2.eagle.org/content/dam/eagle/regulatory-news/2025/Application-of-EU-MRV-and-EU-ETS-to-Offshore-Ships.pdf

*Analytical inference:* This exemption from the ETS MOHA requirement applies only until 2027 for ≥5,000 GT vessels, and the 400–4,999 GT population remains under review for potential future ETS inclusion per the 2026 review deadline.

---
