NYSP (New York State Police): Primary state enforcement agency for commercial vehicle safety in New York. Operates the Commercial Vehicle Enforcement Unit (CVEU) conducting roadside inspections and highway enforcement. NYSDOT (New York State Department of Transportation): Lead MCSAP agency overseeing commercial vehicle safety enforcement, motor carrier registration, NY DOT numbers, and oversize/overweight permitting across six regions statewide. NY DMV (New York State Department of Motor Vehicles): State agency handling IRP registration, IFTA, Highway Use Tax, CDL licensing, and the OSCAR one-stop credentialing system for motor carriers. CVEU (Commercial Vehicle Enforcement Unit): Specialized NYSP unit dedicated to commercial vehicle safety enforcement. Over 100 members certified to perform CVSA inspections, hazardous materials, and cargo tank inspections. OSCAR (One-Stop Credentialing and Registration): New York’s online portal combining IRP, Highway Use Tax, IFTA, and NYSDOT oversize/overweight permits into a single credentialing system for interstate carriers. NY DOT Number: State-level identifier issued by NYSDOT for commercial vehicles operating within New York State. Separate from and in addition to the federal USDOT number. Required for intrastate commercial operations. HUT (Highway Use Tax): New York State tax imposed on motor carriers operating certain commercial vehicles on New York public highways. Separate from federal HVUT. Administered through NY DMV and available via OSCAR. AEB (Automatic Emergency Braking): Safety technology that automatically applies brakes to prevent or reduce collision severity. Becoming more common in commercial vehicles and subject to proposed federal mandates. BIT (Basic Inspection of Terminals): California’s motor carrier terminal inspection program administered by CHP. Evaluates maintenance facilities, safety programs, and record-keeping systems. May apply to New York carriers with California terminals. BOC-3 (Blanket of Coverage): FMCSA form designating process agents in each state where a carrier operates. Required for interstate operating authority (MC number). Must be filed within 90 days of authority application. CDL (Commercial Driver’s License): Required license for drivers operating commercial motor vehicles over certain weight thresholds. New York requires CDL for vehicles 26,001 lbs or more GVWR. Administered by NY DMV. CMV (Commercial Motor Vehicle): In New York under VTL Article 19-B, any vehicle with a gross combination weight rating of more than 10,000 pounds used in commerce to transport property. This threshold is lower than many other states. CSA (Compliance, Safety, Accountability): FMCSA’s safety compliance and enforcement program. Violations add CSA points affecting carrier safety ratings. CVSA (Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance): Nonprofit association developing uniform commercial vehicle safety standards and Out-of-Service criteria used by all states including New York. DataQs: FMCSA’s Data Quality System. Online portal allowing carriers to request review of inspection or crash data they believe contains errors. File at dataqs.fmcsa.dot.gov. DOT (Department of Transportation): Federal agency setting commercial vehicle safety regulations. USDOT numbers identify individual carriers. New York enforces federal DOT regulations through NYSP CVEU and NYSDOT. DVIR (Driver Vehicle Inspection Report): Required pre-trip and post-trip inspection report completed by drivers per 49 CFR 396.11-396.13. Must be retained 3 months. ELD (Electronic Logging Device): Federally mandated device that automatically records driving time and hours of service data. FMCSA (Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration): Federal agency within USDOT responsible for commercial vehicle safety regulation, carrier registration, and enforcement oversight. GVWR (Gross Vehicle Weight Rating): Maximum operating weight of a vehicle as specified by the manufacturer. Critical threshold for regulatory requirements in New York, where CMV definition starts at 10,001 lbs. HOS (Hours of Service): Federal regulations under 49 CFR Part 395 limiting driving and on-duty time for commercial vehicle operators. Enforced in New York by NYSP and NYSDOT. IRP (International Registration Plan): Registration agreement between US states and Canadian provinces for commercial vehicles operating across jurisdictions. Administered in New York by NY DMV’s International Registration Bureau. IFTA (International Fuel Tax Agreement): Fuel tax agreement simplifying reporting for carriers operating in multiple jurisdictions. Administered in New York by NY DMV. ISS (Inspection Selection System): FMCSA algorithm determining which vehicles get selected for roadside inspection. Score based on CSA data, OOS rates, and compliance history. MCSAP (Motor Carrier Safety Assistance Program): Federal grant program funding state commercial vehicle safety enforcement. NYSDOT is New York’s lead MCSAP agency, with NYSP as the primary subrecipient. OOS (Out-of-Service): Order prohibiting vehicle or driver operation until cited safety defects are corrected. Issued when critical safety violations are found during inspection. UCR (Unified Carrier Registration): Annual registration required for interstate motor carriers, brokers, freight forwarders, and leasing companies. Fees based on fleet size. VTL (Vehicle and Traffic Law): New York State Vehicle and Traffic Law. The primary state statute governing commercial vehicle operations, size/weight limits, and equipment requirements in New York. ↑ Contents ← Prev Next → ↑ Contents ← Prev QUICK REFERENCE 17 SECTION 17 OF 17 Government and Regulatory Resources Direct access to New York and federal agencies, regulations, and compliance tools for DOT requirements. 🏛️ New York State Resources ✓ All government resource links verified March 2026. A USDOT number is a unique identifier issued by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) for tracking a company’s safety and compliance records. Prepare for the New Entrant Safety Audit All new carriers must undergo a safety audit within their first 18 months of operation. Broker of Household Goods (HHG) This authority is for individuals or companies arranging the transportation of household goods by authorized carriers. Brokers must meet requirements similar to those for household goods motor carriers, including facilitating packing and unpacking services. New York DOT Number | Moving Authority Arbitration Interstate Tariff BOC-3 Agent All Permits & Services Search Sign in +1 (702) 333-2430 Call Us Sign in Services Arbitration Interstate Tariff BOC-3 Agent All Permits & Services USDOT Number MC Number UCR Registration IRP Registration Search New York DOT Number Understanding the New York DOT Number A New York DOT Number is a unique identifier issued by the New York State Department of Transportation (NYSDOT) through the Intrastate Motor Carrier Registration. Established in the late 1980s to address state-specific safety and regulatory needs, it is required for carriers operating solely within New York, including trucking companies, delivery services, and passenger transport operators meeting weight or cargo criteria. Unlike a USDOT Number, which applies nationwide, the New York DOT Number ensures legal compliance, helps avoid fines, and enhances professional credibility. The state enforces compliance through audits and roadside inspections, examining over 25,000 intrastate vehicles annually, with about 10% cited for violations. For example, Empire Freight Lines, an upstate trucking company, avoided fines during a 2023 NYSDOT audit by maintaining full registration. Beyond legal protection, the number provides benefits like eligibility for state contracts and smoother inspections, making it essential for safe and professional operations within New York. Who Needs a New York DOT Number? Not all commercial vehicle operators in New York require a New York DOT Number, but many do. It ensures compliance with state-specific regulations and helps the Department of Transportation monitor safety and operations. Whether you need one depends on your vehicle type, weight, passenger count, and the materials you transport. Vehicle Types and Operational Thresholds You generally need a New York DOT Number if you: Operate vehicles over 18,000 pounds GVWR – for intrastate use. Transport hazardous materials requiring placards under state law. Carry 8 or more passengers for hire, including limousines, charter buses, and shuttles. Examples of Affected Businesses School and daycare buses Delivery fleets exceeding 18,000 pounds GVWR Limousine and shuttle services Fuel or chemical transport companies Local regulations may impose additional requirements, especially in New York City. Quick Self-Assessment Checklist Ask yourself: Does my vehicle exceed 18,000 pounds GVWR? Do I carry hazardous materials that require placards? Do I transport 8 or more passengers for hire? Am I operating intrastate in New York? If yes to any, you likely need a New York DOT Number. Regulatory Guidance The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) notes that “all commercial motor carriers operating intrastate in New York must register with the state if their vehicle type and operation meet specified thresholds.” NYDOT officials emphasize that “even operators with a federal USDOT Number may need a separate New York DOT registration for intrastate compliance.” General Overview of the Application Process Obtaining a New York DOT Number requires submitting detailed information about your business and commercial vehicles to the New York State Department of Transportation (NYSDOT). While procedures may vary depending on fleet size, vehicle type, and operation classification, accuracy in your records is essential to ensure compliance and prevent operational delays. Required Forms To begin the application, businesses must complete specific NYSDOT forms: Form MCS-150 (Motor Carrier Identification Report): This form provides information about your business, the types of operations you conduct, and the number of vehicles in your fleet. Form MCS-150B (for updates or changes): Used to update existing DOT registration information. Form BOC-3 (Designation of Process Agents): Required for businesses operating interstate, designating agents in each state to receive legal documents. Additional forms may be necessary for specialized operations, such as hazardous materials transport or passenger services. Consulting the NYSDOT website ensures you complete the correct documentation. Processing Time and Fees On average, the NYSDOT processes applications within 7–10 business days for straightforward filings. More complex cases or large fleets may take 2–3 weeks. Fees vary depending on the type and size of the operation: Standard DOT Number applications generally have no direct fee, but additional permits or endorsements may incur costs ranging from $25 to $300. Interstate carriers transporting hazardous materials or passengers often face higher fees due to required endorsements. Common Mistakes to Avoid Even small errors can delay your DOT registration. Frequent issues include: Incomplete or inaccurate addresses: Example – listing a P.O. Box instead of a physical business location. Incorrect vehicle classification: Example – registering a 10,000 lb. truck as “private passenger” instead of “commercial vehicle.” Failure to update information: Example – expanding your fleet without submitting MCS-150B updates, which may lead to fines. To prevent these mistakes, carefully review all forms, double-check fleet details, and maintain an updated record of operational changes. Real-World Example One small logistics company based in Albany, NY, shared their experience: “We initially submitted our MCS-150 with outdated vehicle information, which delayed our registration by two weeks. After consulting a motor carrier compliance professional and resubmitting the corrected forms, we received our NY DOT Number within a week. Accurate record-keeping saved us time and avoided potential fines.” Compliance and Regulations Maintaining a New York Department of Transportation (NYSDOT) Number requires ongoing, detailed adherence to state and federal regulations, not simply a one‑time registration. Compliance ensures your operation remains safe, efficient, and free from costly enforcement actions. Scheduled Inspections and Audits Commercial vehicles operating under a NYSDOT number must undergo annual vehicle safety inspections performed by certified inspectors. These inspections cover brakes, lights, tires, steering, and emissions systems to ensure vehicles are safe for highway operation. In addition to annual vehicle inspections, motor carriers are subject to a biennial (every 24 months) New York State DOT Safety Audit. During this audit, regulators examine your company’s: Driver qualification files Hours‑of‑service logs Accident records Maintenance and inspection documentation Consequences of Non‑Compliance NYSDOT and the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) can impose escalating penalties for failure to comply with inspection and reporting requirements: Fines range from several hundred to several thousand dollars per violation , depending on severity and recurrence. Suspension or revocation of operating authority may occur if critical safety violations are found or if required records cannot be produced during an audit. A 2023 industry report found that over 15% of carriers audited in New York received out‑of‑service orders due to document or maintenance violations. (Note: industry reports may vary by year and source.) Actionable Compliance Tips To stay ahead of audit issues and inspection failures: Schedule and document all annual inspections at least 30 days before the due date. Maintain copies of inspection certificates in both paper and digital formats. Implement a regular internal audit process every quarter to review driver logs, qualification files, and hours‑of‑service records. Train staff on regulatory deadlines and require drivers to submit vehicle defect reports at the end of each shift. Use a central compliance checklist that tracks key compliance deadlines, including inspection dates, audit windows, drug and alcohol testing records, and license renewals. Expert Insight According to Maria Sanchez, a New York‑based fleet compliance officer with 15 years of experience, “Proactive documentation and routine internal reviews are the single most effective ways carriers can avoid regulatory penalties. Waiting for an official audit to review your files is like waiting for a fire alarm before checking your smoke detectors.” Renewal and Updates for New York DOT Number Importance of Keeping Your DOT Information Current While New York DOT Numbers do not require a traditional annual renewal like some permits, carriers are legally obligated to keep their information current with the New York State Department of Transportation (NYSDOT). Updates should be submitted immediately whenever significant operational changes occur, such as: Change in business ownership Change of mailing or business address Addition or removal of commercial vehicles Failing to update records promptly can lead to compliance issues, fines, or even suspension of operating authority. Fees and Filing Considerations Although there is no fixed renewal fee for maintaining a DOT Number itself, certain filings—like updating vehicle or insurance records—may incur administrative costs depending on the type of submission. For example, updating the vehicle fleet size could require submitting forms along with: Vehicle registration fees Safety filing fees Real-Life Consequences of Outdated Information A real-world example illustrates the risks: a small logistics company in New York was fined after failing to update its DOT records to reflect new trucks in its fleet. When an inspector discovered the discrepancy during a roadside audit, the company faced: Financial penalties Temporary suspension of operations Requirement to correct records before resuming business Tips for Staying Compliant To prevent compliance issues, carriers should integrate reminders into their business workflow. Practical strategies include: Using calendar alerts for periodic record reviews Setting recurring tasks in fleet management or operations software Assigning a staff member to monitor and submit updates immediately when operational changes occur Partner with Moving Authority and streamline your journey to obtaining and maintaining your New York DOT Number. Required Permits and Licenses for Commercial Trucks in New York Home About Us Tutorials Services Blog (518) 405-6417 Get UCR now Get a NYHUT account Login Required Permits and Licenses for Commercial Trucks in New York Nov. 11, 2025, 6:18 p.m. Operating a commercial truck in New York involves more than simply registering your vehicle and getting on the road. The state enforces strict permitting and licensing requirements to ensure safety, protect infrastructure, and maintain fair commerce. Whether you’re an independent owner-operator or managing a large fleet, understanding these requirements is key to staying compliant and avoiding costly penalties. 1. Commercial Driver’s License (CDL) Every driver operating a vehicle weighing 26,001 pounds or more , or carrying hazardous materials or passengers, must hold a valid CDL issued by the New York State Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) . CDL Classes: Class A: For combination vehicles (e.g., tractor-trailers). Class B: For single vehicles over 26,000 pounds (e.g., box trucks, dump trucks). Class C: For vehicles carrying hazardous materials or more than 16 passengers. Endorsements: Additional testing is required for endorsements such as: H: Hazardous materials N: Tank vehicles P: Passenger transport T: Double/triple trailers 2. USDOT and NYSDOT Numbers If you operate a commercial vehicle in interstate commerce , you must obtain a USDOT number from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA). If your operations are within New York State only (intrastate) and meet certain criteria—such as vehicles over 10,000 lbs GVW—you’ll also need a New York State DOT (NYSDOT) number . This number identifies your business for safety monitoring and compliance audits. 3. Unified Carrier Registration (UCR) All trucking companies engaged in interstate operations must register under the Unified Carrier Registration (UCR) program each year. The UCR verifies that your company has proper insurance and active DOT registration. Failure to register can lead to fines up to $1,000 per truck . 4. International Registration Plan (IRP) If you operate across state or international borders, you’ll need to register under the IRP , which allows apportioned registration of commercial vehicles among multiple jurisdictions. This ensures that registration fees are distributed fairly based on where the vehicle operates. 5. International Fuel Tax Agreement (IFTA) For vehicles traveling across state lines and weighing over 26,000 pounds , New York requires participation in IFTA . This program simplifies fuel tax reporting—drivers report all miles and fuel purchases quarterly instead of filing in each state separately. 6. Highway Use Tax (HUT) Permit All motor carriers operating trucks weighing more than 18,000 pounds on New York’s public highways must obtain a Highway Use Tax (HUT) Certificate of Registration and display a HUT decal . The HUT tax is based on mileage driven in New York and helps fund road maintenance. Carriers file quarterly HUT returns to report usage. 7. Oversize and Overweight Permits Loads exceeding the standard size or weight limits require special permits issued by the New York State Department of Transportation (NYSDOT) . These permits specify: Allowed dimensions and weight Approved travel routes Time restrictions (e.g., daylight hours only) Special permits are also needed for unique cargo such as construction machinery , wind turbines , or manufactured homes . 8. Special NYC Truck Permits New York City enforces additional rules through the NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) . Trucks operating within the five boroughs must: Use designated truck routes Comply with bridge and tunnel restrictions Obtain special oversize load permits for NYC-specific roads Failure to comply may lead to fines or impoundment. 9. Proof of Insurance and Safety Compliance Before any permits or registrations are approved, carriers must maintain: Public liability insurance (minimum coverage depends on vehicle type and cargo) Cargo insurance (for freight carriers) Vehicle inspection and maintenance records Safety compliance with FMCSA regulations is mandatory for all commercial operators. 10. Other Industry-Specific Permits Depending on your operations, you may also need: Hazardous Materials Safety Permit (for hauling hazardous goods) Agricultural or Farm Vehicle Exemptions Temporary Trip or Fuel Permits (for short-term interstate travel) Conclusion Compliance with New York’s trucking permit and licensing requirements ensures smooth operations and helps avoid penalties that can disrupt business. From your CDL to the HUT permit, each credential plays an essential role in maintaining safe and lawful transportation across the Empire State. Understanding these rules—and staying updated on regulatory changes—keeps your business running efficiently and legally on New York’s busy highways. sections.md:
### The NEPN Framework: What It Is

*Analytical inference:* "The NEPN is Slovenia's main strategic document for energy and climate policy over a ten-year period, aligned with long-term climate goals." *Source: ceenergynews.com/climate/slovenia-new-nepn-2030-2040/, CEE Energy News, May 13, 2026.*

*Analytical inference:* "Member States must submit a draft updated NEPN to the European Commission by 1 January 2028 and adopt the final version by 1 January 2029." *Source: ceenergynews.com/climate/slovenia-new-nepn-2030-2040/, CEE Energy News, May 13, 2026.*

FACT: The National Energy and Climate Plans "are an essential strategic planning tool to deliver a fair, resilient, and climate-neutral Europe, and to steer the much-needed investments for the climate and energy transition, helping to mobilise private and public spending." *Source: commission.europa.eu/energy-climate-change-environment/implementation-eu-countries/energy-and-climate-governance-and-reporting/national-energy-and-climate-plans_en, European Commission, accessed 2026.*

FACT: The NECPs "are required under the Regulation (EU) 2018/1999 on the governance of the energy union and climate action (Governance Regulation)." *Source: commission.europa.eu/energy-climate-change-environment/implementation-eu-countries/energy-and-climate-governance-and-reporting/national-energy-and-climate-plans_en, European Commission, accessed 2026.*

FACT: The NECPs "define how EU countries will tackle the five dimensions of the Energy Union: decarbonisation, energy efficiency, energy security, internal energy market, research, innovation and competitiveness." *Source: commission.europa.eu/energy-climate-change-environment/implementation-eu-countries/energy-and-climate-governance-and-reporting/national-energy-and-climate-plans_en, European Commission, accessed 2026.*

**Effective date (required slot):** FACT: The operative NEPN for Slovenia is the updated Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan for 2021–2030, adopted by the Slovenian government in December 2024. *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.* The NEPN 2030–2040 preparation was initiated in May 2026; no effective date has been established for that instrument as it does not yet exist as an enacted document.

**Jurisdictional scope (required slot):** FACT: The NEPN framework applies to the Republic of Slovenia, as a member state of the European Union, under the EU Governance Regulation (EU) 2018/1999. The operative NEPN sets targets for Slovenian energy and climate policy through 2030, with the new cycle targeting 2030–2040. *Source: ceenergynews.com/climate/slovenia-new-nepn-2030-2040/, CEE Energy News, May 13, 2026; commission.europa.eu/energy-climate-change-environment/implementation-eu-countries/energy-and-climate-governance-and-reporting/national-energy-and-climate-plans_en, European Commission, accessed 2026.*

*Analytical inference:* **Primary deadline (required slot):** FACT: "Member States must submit a draft updated NEPN to the European Commission by 1 January 2028 and adopt the final version by 1 January 2029." *Source: ceenergynews.com/climate/slovenia-new-nepn-2030-2040/, CEE Energy News, May 13, 2026.* These are the binding submission deadlines under the EU Governance Regulation for the next NEPN cycle.

**Penalty summary (required slot):** No penalty provision: the NEPN itself is a national strategic planning instrument; no direct financial penalty on private-sector actors for the NEPN's own framework has been identified in the source corpus as of May 2026. *Specific penalty figure not available from primary sources as of May 2026.* However, the substantive sector-specific targets within the NEPN are implemented through regulations (EU ETS, national building codes, transport regulations, fuel mandates) that carry their own enforcement mechanisms. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any specific implementing measure under the NEPN creates direct compliance obligations and penalties for freight forwarding or logistics operators requires legal review against those implementing instruments individually.

### Why This Framework Is Relevant to the Workspace

The NEPN and its targets set the policy trajectory for the energy, transport, buildings, and industry sectors in Slovenia over a ten-year horizon. For workspaces operating freight, logistics, or supply chain services in or through Slovenia, the NEPN's targets drive:

*Operational implication:* Renewable energy mandates, transport decarbonisation targets, and fuel policy changes established in the NEPN flow into regulations that affect road, rail, and air freight operations, fleet economics, and client sustainability commitments on Slovenia-touching trade lanes.

*Operational implication:* The NEPN's trajectory on transport-sector renewables (a targeted share of 25.8% of renewables in transportation by 2030, sourced below) and its investment requirements in grid, hydrogen infrastructure, and alternative fuels set the regulatory backdrop for fuel cost planning, vehicle specification, and green logistics claims for Slovenia-origin or Slovenia-transiting cargo.

*Operational implication:* For workspaces managing client sustainability reporting obligations (e.g., CSRD, ISO 14083), Slovenia's NEPN targets define the national policy baseline against which Slovenian supplier, carrier, and infrastructure emissions are assessed.

---

This document provides a framework intelligence brief on Slovenia's initiation of its National Energy and Climate Plan (NEPN) for the period 2030–2040, as commenced by the Ministry of Environment, Climate and Energy (now reorganised as the Ministry of Environment and Spatial Planning following a June 2026 government restructuring). The brief covers: the planning framework, its relationship to EU Governance Regulation obligations, the current phase of preparation, the substantive targets established in the preceding updated NEPN (2021–2030, adopted December 2024), and the forward-intelligence picture for the 2030–2040 cycle now under preparation.

**Convention notes:**
- The Slovenian ministry responsible for this framework was, at the time of the NEPN 2021–2030 adoption, the Ministry of Environment, Climate and Energy (MOPE). Following a government reorganisation effective June 2026, responsibilities have been redistributed; energy matters moved to the Ministry of Infrastructure and Energy and the environment/spatial planning portfolio to the Ministry of Environment and Spatial Planning. *Source: gov.si/drzavni-organi/ministrstva/ministrstvo-za-okolje-podnebje-in-energijo, Government of Slovenia, June 2026.*
- The NEPN is referred to in Slovenian as the "Integriran nacionalni energetski in podnebni načrt" (NEPN). In EU nomenclature it is the National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP). Both acronyms refer to the same instrument and are used interchangeably in this document.
- The NEPN 2030–2040 is in the earliest analytical/consultation phase as of the date of this brief (May 2026). No draft text has been published. The 2021–2030 updated NEPN (adopted December 2024) is the operative document.

**Effective date slot:** See Section 2 and Section 14 for required slot coverage.

---

### For Workspaces with Slovenian Road Freight Operations

*Operational implication:* The NEPN's transport-sector renewables target (10.8% → 25.8% by 2030) and fossil fuel subsidy phase-out will progressively change the economics of diesel-powered road freight in Slovenia. Workspaces should:

*Analytical inference:* 1. **Map carrier fleet composition** on Slovenia-touching routes: identify the share of Euro VI diesel, electric, or alternative-fuel vehicles currently used and the carrier's electrification roadmap.
2. **Assess fuel cost exposure**: as fossil fuel subsidies phase out by 2030, the unsubsidised cost of diesel on Slovenian routes will increase. *Specific future cost delta not available from primary sources as of May 2026.*
3. **Track alternative fuel infrastructure development**: the NEPN envisages EUR 223 million in hydrogen infrastructure by 2030. *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.* The pace of deployment will determine whether hydrogen or electric vehicle charging infrastructure is practically available for freight operations within the plan period.

### For Workspaces Managing Slovenian Warehouse or Facility Operations

*Operational implication:* The NEPN's buildings emissions target (70% reduction by 2030) and 55% renewables-in-buildings target may flow into implementing regulations requiring energy renovation of commercial buildings. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any enacted implementing regulation under the NEPN creates an obligation on commercial property operators (including logistics warehouses) to meet specific energy performance standards requires legal review against Slovenian building energy performance regulations.

### For Workspaces with Sustainability Reporting Obligations

*Operational implication:* Track Slovenia's NEPN progress reports and Commission assessments as primary sources for national emission factors and energy mix data. The biennial reporting cycle (next report expected approximately 2025 data, published 2026) provides the most authoritative update to national-level parameters used in ISO 14083 or CSRD supply chain calculations for Slovenia.

### Government Reorganisation Adjustment (immediate)

Assess internal processes for Slovenian regulatory engagement and update contact lists to reflect the post-June 2026 ministerial structure. The energy and transport NEPN portfolio has moved to the Ministry of Infrastructure and Energy; the environment portfolio to the Ministry of Environment and Spatial Planning. *Source: gov.si/drzavni-organi/ministrstva/ministrstvo-za-okolje-podnebje-in-energijo, Government of Slovenia, June 2026.*

---

**MONITORING — NEPN 2030–2040 Consultation Phase Open**

*Analytical inference:* Engage the public consultation process on NEPN 2030–2040 long-term scenarios now, if the workspace has Slovenia-routed operations or Slovenian-sourced cargo.

*Operational implication:* FACT: Slovenia "has started preparing its new National Energy and Climate Plan (NEPN) for 2030–2040 and is inviting the public and experts to take part in a consultation on long-term scenarios that will form the basis of future energy and climate policy." *Source: ceenergynews.com/climate/slovenia-new-nepn-2030-2040/, CEE Energy News, May 13, 2026.* For workspaces whose clients or principals operate in Slovenian energy-intensive sectors (industry, transport, buildings), the scenario framing now open for consultation will shape investment and fuel decisions through 2040.

Action: Identify whether commercial clients or principals active in Slovenia have a stake in the scenario selection (e.g., logistics infrastructure investment, fleet electrification, hydrogen adoption); if so, commission a review of which scenario aligns with their investment horizon and brief commercial leadership before the consultation window closes.

Re-check window: Monitor for publication of draft long-term scenarios (expected late 2026 or 2027, per industry-standard NEPN preparation timelines — *Analytical inference:* based on the January 2028 draft submission deadline and typical 12–18 month scenario-to-draft lead time; no published schedule for the scenario consultation closing date has been identified in the source corpus as of May 2026).

---

**MONITORING — Operative 2021–2030 NEPN Targets Now Baseline for Client Claims**

*Analytical inference:* Map workspace operations against the adopted NEPN 2021–2030 targets to validate any green logistics or sustainability claims made to Slovenian or Slovenia-related clients.

*Operational implication:* The NEPN 2021–2030 (adopted December 2024) sets sectoral targets that are now the operative national policy baseline. Claims referencing Slovenia's energy transition, renewable energy infrastructure, or transport decarbonisation must be traceable to the adopted plan's figures — not to prior draft versions. The Balkan Green Energy News analysis notes that the August 2024 draft showed improvement but that the final document adopted December 2024 is the authoritative version. *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

Action: Verify that any client-facing sustainability documentation referencing Slovenian energy or transport policy is updated to cite the December 2024 adopted NEPN, not the 2023 draft or the 2019 original.

---

**MONITORING — Government Reorganisation: Track Ministerial Responsibility**

Verify which ministry now holds competence over energy and climate plan implementation for each engagement.

FACT: Following the June 2026 government reorganisation, "področje energetike, oskrbe z naftnimi derivati in infrastrukture za alternativna goriva v prometu, trajnostno mobilnost, celostno prometno načrtovanje in javni potniški promet v notranjem in čezmejnem prometu po novem sodi med pristojnosti Ministrstva za infrastrukturo in energetiko" (the field of energy, petroleum product supply and alternative fuel infrastructure in transport, sustainable mobility, integrated transport planning and public passenger transport now falls under the Ministry of Infrastructure and Energy). *Source: gov.si/drzavni-organi/ministrstva/ministrstvo-za-okolje-podnebje-in-energijo, Government of Slovenia, June 2026.*

*Operational implication:* For workspaces engaging Slovenian government counterparts on transport fuel policy, alternative fuel infrastructure, or NEPN implementation, the responsible ministry has changed. Contacts and official channels established under the former Ministry of Environment, Climate and Energy for energy-transport matters now sit under a different ministry.

Action: Update stakeholder maps and correspondence routing for any Slovenia-related regulatory engagement immediately.

---

*Section 13 — Conditional.*

**CAN Europe Civil Society Assessment (August 2024 draft):**

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "Slovenia's draft NECP update falls short of aligning with a 1.5°C target, lacking concrete measures or policies." FACT: "As of 2022, Slovenia was not fully on track to implement its old 2019 NECP, whose ambition is now obsolete." *Source: 1point5.caneurope.org/countries/slovenia/, CAN Europe Together for 1.5°C, accessed 2026.*

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "Slovenia is slightly below expectations of the 2019 NECP when it comes to the share of renewables in final energy consumption." *Source: 1point5.caneurope.org/countries/slovenia/, CAN Europe Together for 1.5°C, accessed 2026.*

*Analytical inference:* The civil society analysis, based on the August 2024 draft, raises a credible concern about implementation deficit that may be relevant to workspaces making forward-looking green logistics claims premised on Slovenia meeting its NEPN targets on schedule.

**LULUCF Sector Concern:**

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "While both gross and net emissions were on a declining trend, emissions from the LULUCF sector raise concerns: values have worsened every year since 2019." *Source: 1point5.caneurope.org/countries/slovenia/, CAN Europe Together for 1.5°C, accessed 2026.*

*Analytical inference:* LULUCF deterioration is not directly relevant to freight operations but is relevant to workspaces offering nature-based offset or carbon sequestration services referencing Slovenian forestry, as the policy trajectory on forest management in Slovenia is under pressure.

**2030–2040 Scenario Design Parameters:**

FACT: "These scenarios are based on two key commitments: the European Union's target of a 90 per cent net emissions reduction by 2040 compared to 1990 levels, and Slovenia's national commitment to achieve climate neutrality by 2045." *Source: ceenergynews.com/climate/slovenia-new-nepn-2030-2040/, CEE Energy News, May 13, 2026.*

*Analytical inference:* The 90% net emissions reduction target for 2040 (EU level) is a more ambitious stepping-stone than the 55% 2030 target. For workspaces planning infrastructure or fleet investments with 10–15 year useful lives, the 2040 target implies that assets committed by 2027–2028 must be compatible with a near-zero-carbon operating environment by end of life.

---

*Note: This section covers the substantive targets and obligations established in the operative NEPN 2021–2030 that are relevant to freight and logistics operations. The NEPN 2030–2040 has not yet established targets; this section will require full revision once the draft is published (expected 1 January 2028).*

*Analytical inference:* ### 1. Transport Sector Renewables Trajectory (per-year not available; 2030 endpoint sourced)

FACT: The renewables share in transportation "advances to 25.8% from 10.8%" by 2030. *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.* The per-year trajectory between baseline and 2030 endpoint is not specified in the source corpus. *Specific annual interim milestones not available from primary sources as of May 2026.*

*Operational implication:* For workspaces with road freight operations in or through Slovenia, a 2.4× increase in required renewable transport fuel content from 2024 to 2030 implies progressive tightening of fuel blend requirements and electrification pressure on the fleet of carriers used.

*Analytical inference:* ### 2. Fossil Fuel Subsidy Phase-Out (by 2030)

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "The plan stipulates ending fossil fuel subsidies by the end of the period." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.* The mechanism, timeline of phase-out steps, and scope of subsidies covered are not detailed in the source corpus. *Specific phase-out mechanism not available from primary sources as of May 2026.*

### 3. GHG Emissions — Buildings (by 2030)

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "Slovenia now aspires to cut emissions in buildings by at least 70%." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.* Relevant for workspaces operating Slovenian warehouse or office facilities subject to building energy performance implementing regulations.

*Analytical inference:* ### 4. Overall Emissions Trajectory (with coal exit qualifier)

*Analytical inference:* The NEPN targets a 55% emissions reduction (against 2005 baseline) but with Slovenia achieving this by 2033 via coal exit, not by 2030. The previously operative target was 36%. *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

### 5. Non-ETS Sector Trajectory (background)

*Analytical inference:* "Slovenia is also off the decarbonisation trajectory projected in the 2019 NECP for non-ETS sectors, with 2022 values surpassing pre-pandemic levels (11.1 MtCO2-eq compared to 10.8 in 2019). The available data indicates that the transport sector is an important component of this surge in emissions." *Source: 1point5.caneurope.org/countries/slovenia/, CAN Europe Together for 1.5°C, accessed 2026.*

*Operational implication:* The transport sector's role in Slovenia's non-ETS overrun signals that regulatory pressure on transport emissions will increase as the 2030 deadline approaches — consistent with the NEPN's 25.8% renewables-in-transport target and the fossil fuel subsidy phase-out commitment.

### 6. Alignment with EU Fit for 55 and REPowerEU

*Analytical inference:* "The plan aligns with the European Union's packages Fit for 55 and REPowerEU." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

FACT: The NEPN 2030–2040 scenarios "are based on two key commitments: the European Union's target of a 90 per cent net emissions reduction by 2040 compared to 1990 levels, and Slovenia's national commitment to achieve climate neutrality by 2045." *Source: ceenergynews.com/climate/slovenia-new-nepn-2030-2040/, CEE Energy News, May 13, 2026.*

### 7. EU Governance Regulation Reporting Requirement

FACT: "Each country shall submit a progress report every 2 years, according to the structure, format, technical details and process set out in the Implementing Regulation." *Source: commission.europa.eu/energy-climate-change-environment/implementation-eu-countries/energy-and-climate-governance-and-reporting/national-energy-and-climate-plans_en, European Commission, accessed 2026.*

The NEPN 2030–2040 does not yet exist as an authoritative guidance document. This section covers the adopted 2021–2030 NEPN's key provisions as the operative baseline.

### GHG Emissions Targets

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "The Fit-for-55 goal of a 55% drop in emissions is for 2030. Slovenia aims to achieve it only by 2033, the deadline it set for quitting the use of coal." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "The previous target was 36% and the baseline is the 2005 level. Slovenia now aspires to cut emissions in buildings by at least 70%." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

*Analytical inference:* Slovenia's emissions trajectory lags the EU's 2030 headline by approximately three years (achieving 55% reduction by 2033 rather than 2030). For workspaces reporting Scope 3 emissions from Slovenian supply chain nodes, the national trajectory implies slower decarbonisation of the Slovenian electricity grid and transport infrastructure than the EU average, which may affect the emissions intensity factors used in client reporting.

*Analytical inference:* ### Energy Consumption Target

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "Gross final energy consumption in 2030 is determined at a maximum of 50.2 TWh, compared to 54.9 TWh in the initial document, adopted in 2020." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

### Renewables Targets (with per-sector breakdown)

*Analytical inference:* The NEPN targets "a share of renewables in gross final energy consumption [of] 33%." FACT: The breakdown: "renewable sources need to amount to 55.4% [in electricity], against 40.7% projected for this year [2024]. The share in heating and cooling grows to 45.2% from 36.3% while in transportation it advances to 25.8% from 10.8%." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

*Analytical inference:* "Slovenia managed to reach its EU-mandated 25% share [of renewables in gross final energy consumption] in 2022, or 25.4% to be exact, through a so-called statistical transfer with neighboring Croatia." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

FACT: "The buildings sector's goal is 55% while industrial production, including waste heat, needs to reach 30%, the NECP reads." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

*Operational implication:* The transport-sector renewables target rising from approximately 10.8% (2024 baseline) to 25.8% by 2030 signals a doubling of the required renewable content in transport fuels — a trajectory that drives both road fleet electrification requirements and alternative fuel mandates affecting freight vehicles operating in Slovenia.

### Fossil Fuel Subsidy Phase-Out

*Analytical inference:* "The plan stipulates ending fossil fuel subsidies by the end of the period [2030]." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

*Operational implication:* For workspaces operating road freight in Slovenia, the planned phase-out of fossil fuel subsidies by 2030 signals upward pressure on diesel costs as the decade progresses. The pace and mechanism of subsidy removal are not specified in the source corpus.

### Investment Framework

*Analytical inference:* "The scenario with additional measures in Slovenia's updated Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) envisages EUR 57 billion in investment from 2021 until the end of the decade. The government adopted the final document, which envisages EUR 22 billion for energy and climate targets in particular. The biggest chunk, EUR 5.4 billion, is for households, with measures including energy renovation and the replacement of devices. Electricity distribution and transmission grids are entitled to EUR 4 billion, followed by distributed electricity generation from renewable sources, EUR 3.8 billion." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "Total public sector investments 2021–2030 are estimated at EUR 6.9 billion." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

*Analytical inference:* ### Energy Storage and Grid

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "There is a need for 400 MW in batteries, 100 MW in electrolyzers and more pumped storage hydropower capacity, though the references to the Kozjak project were deleted." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "Another pumped storage hydropower plant is seen by 2045. It would be able to generate 180 MW and store 2.6 GWh." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "The Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan envisages an overall 500 MW in gas power plants in Slovenia by the end of the decade." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

### Hydrogen Infrastructure

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "Projected investments in hydrogen infrastructure by 2030 are EUR 223 million, of which nearly the entire amount is for a pipeline system and electrolyzers. The green hydrogen production capacity goal is 100 MW." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

### Nuclear Energy

*Analytical inference:* "The document's authors reiterated that 'a quality and transparent decision' needs to be reached by 2028 on the proposal to build Slovenia's second conventional nuclear power plant by 2040. The reference capacity in the related scenario is 1.1 GW, from a range of 1 GW to 2.4 GW. A small modular reactor (SMR), of 250 MW, would come online by mid-century, the NECP reads." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "Slovenia aims to decide by 2028 whether it will build its second nuclear power plant." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

### Electricity Security of Supply

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "Slovenia plans to maintain a high level of electricity connectivity with neighboring countries, with a goal of more than 80%. At least 85% of power supply needs to be from domestic sources in 2030 and 100% by 2040, the government said. Another target for the current decade is to cover at least 75% of electricity demand in the transmission network, during peak load hours, with domestic production. After 2033 the level is 80%." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.*

### Civil Society Assessment of Plan Adequacy

FACT: "The latest Slovenian NECP draft (August 2024) shows some improvement over the 2023 draft version but still falls short of Paris Agreement commitments. A key issue is the weak renewable energy target, falling over 10% below the EU Commission's recommendation." *Source: 1point5.caneurope.org/countries/slovenia/, CAN Europe Together for 1.5°C, accessed 2026.*

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "GHG emission reduction targets remain unchanged from the 2023 version, while final and primary energy reduction targets have improved but still fall short of Paris Agreement requirements. Another major issue is the substantial weakening of fossil fuel subsidy phase-out measures and targets compared to the 2023 draft and the currently valid 2019 NECP." *Source: 1point5.caneurope.org/countries/slovenia/, CAN Europe Together for 1.5°C, accessed 2026.*

**Statistical Transfer Mechanism (precedent established):** FACT: Slovenia used a statistical transfer with Croatia in 2022 to meet its EU-mandated 25% renewables share. *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.* This mechanism is provided for under EU renewables law and allows Member States to count renewable energy produced in another Member State toward their own target through a bilateral agreement. *Analytical inference:* If domestic renewable deployment falls short of the 33% 2030 target, Slovenia may seek further statistical transfers — which would affect the "actual" renewable content of Slovenia's energy mix for emissions reporting purposes, creating a gap between reported and physical energy composition.

**TEŠ Early Closure Scenario:** FACT: "Chances are that the country's only coal power plant, Termoelektrarna Šoštanj (TEŠ), and its accompanying mine Premogovnik Velenje, will close within a few years or operate at minimum capacity. Its focus is on district heating, until a cleaner system replaces it." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.* Early TEŠ closure is an edge case that could accelerate Slovenia's emissions trajectory beyond the official NEPN schedule — relevant for forward-looking sustainability claims or investment decisions based on Slovenia's grid emission intensity.

**Nuclear Scenario Qualifier:** FACT: The NEPN contains two "advanced scenarios" — one based on acceleration in renewables and the other on more nuclear energy. The pumped storage hydropower target of 440 MW "matches" both scenarios. *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.* *Analytical inference:* The 2028 nuclear decision creates a bifurcated policy trajectory for Slovenia's post-2030 energy mix, with materially different implications for grid emission factors and energy security on Slovenia-routed operations depending on the decision's outcome.

---

**Question 1: Does the NEPN 2030–2040 itself impose direct obligations on freight operators?**

*Legal Confirmation Required:* The NEPN is a national strategic planning instrument submitted to the EU Commission under the Governance Regulation. The source corpus does not indicate that the NEPN framework itself creates direct, justiciable obligations on private operators. Obligations flow through implementing regulations. Whether any specific implementing measure under the NEPN 2021–2030 or its successor creates direct compliance requirements for freight forwarding, logistics, or transport operations in Slovenia requires legal review against those specific implementing instruments.

**Question 2: Which ministry now holds NEPN implementation authority post-June 2026 reorganisation?**

FACT: Following the June 2026 reorganisation, energy and transport-related NEPN implementation has moved to the Ministry of Infrastructure and Energy; environmental and spatial planning matters remain with the Ministry of Environment and Spatial Planning. *Source: gov.si/drzavni-organi/ministrstva/ministrstvo-za-okolje-podnebje-in-energijo, Government of Slovenia, June 2026.* The allocation of NEPN coordination responsibilities between the two ministries has not been addressed in the source corpus. *Specific allocation not available from primary sources as of June 2026.*

**Question 3: Is Slovenia's 2024 statistical transfer with Croatia repeatable for the 2030 target?**

*Analytical inference:* "Slovenia managed to reach its EU-mandated 25% share [of renewables] in 2022, or 25.4% to be exact, through a so-called statistical transfer with neighboring Croatia." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.* The NEPN does not address whether this mechanism will be used for the higher 2030 target. *Specific provision on future statistical transfers not available from primary sources as of May 2026.*

*Analytical inference:* Reliance on statistical transfers for the larger 2030 gap (from 25.4% achieved in 2022 to 33% target in 2030) is uncertain. If domestic renewable deployment falls short, this question becomes commercially relevant for workspaces claiming Slovenian renewable energy content in their supply chains.

*Analytical inference:* **Question 4: Does Slovenia's coal exit by 2033 affect Slovenian grid electricity emission factors used in Scope 2/3 reporting?**

FACT: "Slovenia aims to achieve [the 55% emissions reduction] only by 2033, the deadline it set for quitting the use of coal." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.* FACT: The coal plant TEŠ (Termoelektrarna Šoštanj) "and its accompanying mine Premogovnik Velenje, will close within a few years or operate at minimum capacity." *Source: balkangreenenergynews.com/slovenia-adopts-updated-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan/, Balkan Green Energy News, December 27, 2024.* *Operational implication:* The prospect of early TEŠ closure means Slovenian grid emission factors may improve faster than the NEPN's official 2033 schedule implies — workspaces should track actual TEŠ operational status rather than relying solely on the policy timeline.

---

The NEPN is a national strategic planning instrument; it does not directly impose obligations on private-sector freight operators by its own force. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any specific obligation under the NEPN's implementing instruments (e.g., transport fuel mandates, fleet decarbonisation rules, green public procurement requirements, building renovation requirements) attaches to the workspace depends on the workspace's operational role (carrier, forwarder, importer, shipper) and the specific implementing measure — each must be assessed individually.

The compliance chain runs as follows (as sourced from the corpus):

1. **EU Governance Regulation (EU) 2018/1999** → obliges Slovenia as a Member State to submit and implement a NEPN. FACT: NECPs are "required under Regulation (EU) 2018/1999." *Source: commission.europa.eu/energy-climate-change-environment/implementation-eu-countries/energy-and-climate-governance-and-reporting/national-energy-and-climate-plans_en, European Commission, accessed 2026.*

2. **Slovenia's NEPN** → translates EU targets into Slovenian sectoral targets and investment frameworks (energy, transport, buildings, industry, hydrogen).

3. **Implementing regulations** → sector-specific rules (fuel blend mandates, ETS, building energy performance codes, transport regulations) create direct obligations on operators. These are distinct instruments not fully enumerated in this brief's source corpus.

4. **Workspace position** → *Legal Confirmation Required:* the workspace's position in the compliance chain (whether as carrier, forwarder, infrastructure user, or fuel purchaser) determines which implementing regulations apply and on whom obligations fall as defined in those instruments.

*Operational implication:* For workspaces handling Slovenian cross-border or domestic freight, the NEPN's transport targets (25.8% renewables in transport by 2030; fossil fuel subsidy phase-out by 2030; 500 MW gas power capacity cap) signal the direction of fuel pricing, infrastructure availability, and regulatory requirements that will flow through to carrier contracts and fuel surcharges on Slovenia-routed shipments.

Highlights Highlights News Press materials Reports PRESS RELEASE: New Report: Blueprint or bust: Europe’s climate targets hinge on implementation PRESS RELEASE: New Report: Blueprint or bust: Europe’s climate targets hinge on implementation The Together for 1.5 consortium is launching its final NECPs assessment report: EU climate goals at risk - NECPs' ambitious implementation must close the gaps that includes a full set of recommendations and country-by-country profiles of the 16 NECPs assessed: Austria, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Malta, Portugal, Slovenia, and Spain. Reports 15th March, 2023 T he current decade is a crucial phase of the Paris Agreement pathway that would allow us to stay within the 1.5°C limit established under the Paris Agreement and thus avoid the worst consequences of the climate crisis. Resources NECP s are National Energy and Climate Plans for 2021-2030 – These fundamental documents combine the targets, policies and measures planned by EU Member States to achieve their climate and energy commitments. JS Bin Tweets by TwitterDev Join the conversation National Energy and Climate Plans for 2021-2030 are fundamental documents that combine the targets, policies and measures planned by EU Member States to achieve their climate and energy commitments. The deadline for Member States to come up with their new draft NECPs – June 2023 – is swiftly approaching. The new final revised plans – which should factor in feedback from the European Commission and views of the public – will then have to be submitted in June 2024 . This revision is an essential moment for EU Member States to set things right – to bring NECPs much closer to their real, transformative potential. More ambitious NECPs should help to keep global warming to 1.5°C, while at the same time ensuring energy security and more equity and justice in Europe. As an European citizen, have your say on your NECP. Follow us on Twitter and join forces for a better, safer, more just Europe. Follow us Country Assessments Click on the countries to see their performance on the implementation of National Energy and Climate Plans. 14 climate and environment NGOs based in thirteen European countries working together to put Europe on track for achieving a safe and stable climate for current and future generations. We are committed to push our governments to accelerate climate action in our countries and to keep them accountable for their actions. Key Messages To the European Commission National Energy and Climate Plans (NECPs) can be a powerful instrument in the EU’s contribution to limit global warming to 1.5°C, while at the same time ensuring energy security and energy justice across the EU. The upcoming NECPs revision, 2023 – 2024, must be prioritised by the European Commission as it is a fundamental opportunity for EU Member States to set things right – to bring NECPs much closer to their real, transformative potential. To national governments You have now a historic opportunity to deliver true change and make the life of the citizens better: keep them safe from climate impacts and sky-rocketing (fossil) energy bills. You need to put all hands on deck and dramatically increase nature-friendly and socially just climate action in the next few years. Speed up energy transformation to increase energy security, address fossil energy crisis and provide clean and affordable energy supply. NECPs are your tool. To concerned ones This project will closely monitor the processes and the plans that our countries will put forward in order to reduce our emissions and transform the way we produce and consume energy. These national plans must help solve the climate, energy and cost of living crisis. We don’t even need a miracle, but just all hands on deck and the political will to go for an accelerated climate action. Together we can make governments act and address dangerous climate change at an accelerated pace. Subscribe to our newsletter and let’s join forces. The opportunity All EU countries have a fundamental opportunity in the revision of their National Energy and Climate Plans, taking place between 2023 and 2024, to set things right and increase their national climate ambition in order to put the EU on track with the Paris Agreement and go for a deep transformation of the way we produce and consume energy. The impact These pathways have a direct impact on us. Not only are they supposed to keep us safe from dangerous climate change impacts (floods, droughts, heatwaves, fires); but also to improve our lives. These plans will determine whether we will receive financial support to insulate our houses or install solar panels and have us stop worrying about our energy bills. National Energy and Climate Plans (NECPs) are the right opportunity to push the fast-forward button and accelerate climate action. Inspiring stories from all over Europe showcase how the just transition can be accelerated, as the deadline for Member States to come up with their new draft NECPs – end of June 2023 – is swiftly approaching. Climate and environment NGOs based in 12 European countries gathered almost one hundred concrete examples of climate action measures implemented on the ground. These should inspire all governments and put Europe on track for achieving a safe and stable climate and to ensure we all harvest the benefits of a sustainable life. By examining the stories of countries taking action, such as promoting clean public transport, advancing renewable energy deployment, greening cities, shortening food supply chains, and combating energy poverty, we can find inspiration. We should urge our governments to include these effective measures in their NECPs and exclude those that civil society deems problematic. Renewables Sustainable Mobility Buildings Greening Cities Agriculture Money for change Community Energy Energy Poverty Just Transition Public Transportation Sufficiency False solutions Renewables Countries are required to communicate their contribution to the binding EU renewables target for 2030 in their NECPs, and they should go beyond the bare minimum. A prosperous and sustainable energy future, fully based on renewable energy is possible, by taking bold actions and boosting the clean energy transition in NECPs. The examples below show the transition is already underway, but we must scale up significantly. Home … Topics Climate action Delivering the European Green Deal Fit for 55: Delivering on the proposals Fit for 55: Delivering on the proposals On the path to climate neutrality Under the European Climate Law, the EU committed to reduce its net greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030. The ‘Fit for 55’ package of legislation makes all sectors of the EU’s economy fit to meet this target. It sets the EU on a path to reach its climate targets in a fair, cost-effective and competitive way. For each of the countries covered, the tool looks into overall and sectoral greenhouse gas emissions reduction pathways and some energy transition indicators . In other words, the tool shows where Member States really stand, what they have promised and how far they are from the minimum EU requirements. By doing so, it provides key information to identify gaps in ambition and implementation of national climate action. Check the key findings and methodology behind the figures. Key findings The October 2024 update of the NECP tracker revelas that: Despite some improvements, the current level of ambition of the latest available NECP updates is insufficient not only to align with Paris Agreement commitments, but also to reach the EU 2030 climate and energy objectives , which would be in breach of the European Climate Law. The implementation of the old 2019 NECPs is lagging behind . All Member States assessed in the tracker seem to show some worrying trends and gaps in keeping up to their pledges. NECPs present varying but overall poor transparency and quality of data , which hinders the plans’ credibility as well as access to information. Home Climate Slovenia begins preparation of NEPN 2030–2040 Climate Powered by Slovenia begins preparation of NEPN 2030–2040 By Emese Fabian May 13, 2026 Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin Email Print Slovenia has started preparing its new National Energy and Climate Plan (NEPN) for 2030- 2040 and is inviting the public and experts to take part in a consultation on long-term scenarios that will form the basis of future energy and climate policy. The NEPN is Slovenia’s main strategic document for energy and climate policy over a ten-year period, aligned with long-term climate goals. Member States must submit a draft updated NEPN to the European Commission by 1 January 2028 and adopt the final version by 1 January 2029. The first step is preparing analytical groundwork, including long-term scenarios for different pathways towards climate neutrality. These scenarios are based on two key commitments: the European Union’s target of a 90 per cent net emissions reduction by 2040 compared to 1990 levels, and Slovenia’s national commitment to achieve climate neutrality by 2045. The period to 2040 is crucial, as it will shape long-lived investment decisions in energy, infrastructure, buildings, industry and transport. Page contents Page contents The process National Energy and Climate plans 2021-2030 Documents The National Energy and Climate Plans (NECPs) are an essential strategic planning tool to deliver a fair, resilient, and climate-neutral Europe, and to steer the much-needed investments for the climate and energy transition, helping to mobilise private and public spending. The NECPs enable each EU country to outline precise actions and policies to achieve the 2030 climate and energy targets and fulfil the broader objectives of the Energy Union. Required under the Regulation (EU)2018/1999 on the governance of the energy union and climate action (Governance Regulation), the NECPs first took shape in 2020 and have since then been updated to incorporate the ambitious targets set by the European Green Deal, the Fit for 55 Package legislation and the RepowerEU plan. The NECPs define how EU countries will tackle the five dimensions of the Energy Union : decarbonisation energy efficiency energy security internal energy market research, innovation and competitiveness These plans necessitate coordinated efforts across government departments, creating a robust framework that catalyses public and private investment and supports a thorough implementation of the agreed policies. Each country shall submit a progress report every 2 years, according to the structure, format, technical details and process set out in the  Implementing Regulation . The Commission will, as part of the  state of the energy union report , monitor the EU's progress as a whole towards achieving these targets. To better develop and implement the plans, Member States were required to consult citizens, businesses and regional authorities in the drafting and finalisation process. The governance regulation also required Member States to submit by the start of 2020 national  long term strategies  looking forward to 2050. NECPs as a governance tool will be reviewed for the post-2030 period as part of the forthcoming revision of the Governance of the Energy Union and Climate Action Regulation. The process The adoption by the Member States of the final NECPS, follow an iterative process with the Commission. Under the Governance Regulation Member States have to submit their NECPs for the period 2021-2030 to the Commission. Member States first submitted their final NECPs in 2019 and then updated them in 2024 to reflect the increased EU 2030 climate and energy ambitions as set by the Fit for 55 legislative package and the RepowerEU plan. Updating the NECPs 2021-2030 On 28 May 2025, the Commission published its EU-wide assessment of the final updated NECPs accompanied by a Staff Working Document with the individual assessment of 23 final updated NECPs submitted and evaluated to that date. The Commission assessment of the final updated plans of Estonia and Slovakia was published on 2 October 2025 and the assessment of the final updated plan of Belgium on 26 January 2026. Member States were due to submit these final updated NECPs by 30 June 2024, taking into account the Commission’s recommendations on the draft updated NECPs. By 30 June 2023, Member States were due to submit their draft updated NECPs in line with article 14 of the Governance Regulation. The Commission had published guidance to Member States on the process and scope of this update in 2022. On 18 December 2023, the Commission published its   EU-wide assessment  of the draft updated NECPs, together with individual assessments and country-specific recommendations for the 21 Member States that submitted their draft plans in time. Six Member States submitted their draft updated NECPs at a later stage. The assessments and recommendations for those countries were published on 23 February 2024, 26 April 2024 and on 18 October 2024. On 24 October 2023, the Commission published its  technical assessment of the first NECP progress reports  towards meeting the EU’s energy and climate objectives. The relevant Staff Working Document is part of the  2023 State of the Energy Union report .  Initial NECPs 2021-2030 Under the Governance Regulation Member States had to submit their draft NECPs for the period 2021-2030 to the Commission by 31 December 2018. These were analysed by the Commission with an  overall assessment  and country-specific recommendations published in June 2019. Taking these recommendations into account, Member States were then required to submit their final NECPs by 31 December 2019. On 17 September 2020, the Commission published a detailed  EU-wide assessment of the final NECPs . As a follow-up, and as part of the 2020 Energy Union report, the Commission published  individual assessments  of each of the national plans with further guidance. Climate Plan Photo: iStock Published December 27, 2024 Update June 3, 2026 Country Slovenia Author Igor Todorović Comments 0 Share Slovenia aims to decide by 2028 whether it will build its second nuclear power plant. The government is targeting a 55.4% share of renewables in electricity, 45.2% in heating and cooling and 25.8% in transportation, according to the updated NECP for 2030. There is a need for 400 MW in batteries, 100 MW in electrolyzers and more pumped storage hydropower capacity, though the references to the Kozjak project were deleted. The scenario with additional measures in Slovenia’s updated Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP or, in Slovenian, NEPN) envisages EUR 57 billion in investment from 2021 until the end of the decade. The government adopted the final document, which envisages EUR 22 billion for energy and climate targets in particular. The biggest chunk, EUR 5.4 billion, is for households, with measures including energy renovation and the replacement of devices. Electricity distribution and transmission grids are entitled to EUR 4 billion, followed by distributed electricity generation from renewable sources, EUR 3.8 billion. Total public sector investments 2021-2030 are estimated at EUR 6.9 billion. The government said the goals are aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions, increasing sustainability, energy independence and security and accelerating the transition to clean energy sources. The plan aligns with the European Union’s packages Fit for 55 and REPowerEU, the announcement adds. Probable early closure of only coal plant would catapult Slovenia to its emissions target The Fit-for-55 goal of a 55% drop in emissions is for 2030. Slovenia aims to achieve it only by 2033, the deadline it set for quitting the use of coal. But chances are that the country’s only coal power plant, Termoelektrarna Šoštanj (TEŠ), and its accompanying mine Premogovnik Velenje, will close within a few years or operate at minimum capacity. Its focus is on district heating, until a cleaner system replaces it. The previous target was 36% and the baseline is the 2005 level. Slovenia now aspires to cut emissions in buildings by at least 70%. Gross final energy consumption in 2030 is determined at a maximum of 50.2 TWh, compared to 54.9 TWh in the initial document, adopted in 2020. The plan stipulates ending fossil fuel subsidies by the end of the period. Industrial production projected to run 30% or more on renewables before end of decade The targeted share of renewables in gross final energy consumption 33%. Of note, Slovenia managed to reach its EU-mandated 25% share in 2022, or 25.4% to be exact, through a so-called statistical transfer with neighboring Croatia. The European Union’s goal for 2030 is 42.5%. The breakdown shows that renewable sources need to amount to 55.4%, against 40.7% projected for this year. The share in heating and cooling grows to 45.2% from 36.3% while in transportation it advances to 25.8% from 10.8%. The buildings sector’s goal is 55% while industrial production, including waste heat, needs to reach 30%, the NECP reads. Slovenia aims to host green hydrogen electrolyzers of at least 100 MW in total in 2030 Projected investments in hydrogen infrastructure by 2030 are EUR 223 million, of which nearly the entire amount is for a pipeline system and electrolyzers. The green hydrogen production capacity goal is 100 MW. The rest of energy storage includes battery energy storage systems (BESS) of 400 MW in total capability. As for pumped storage hydropower plants, the plan is to add 440 MW by 2030 in both advanced scenarios. One is based on acceleration in renewables and the other on more nuclear energy. The capacity matches the Kozjak project. However the references to it were deleted from the draft, which pointed to potential grid connection issues. Another pumped storage hydropower plant is seen by 2045. It would be able to generate 180 MW and store 2.6 GWh. The Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan envisages an overall 500 MW in gas power plants in Slovenia by the end of the decade. One SMR facility seen by 2050 The document’s authors reiterated that “a quality and transparent decision” needs to be reached by 2028 on the proposal to build Slovenia’s second conventional nuclear power plant by 2040. The reference capacity in the related scenario is 1.1 GW, from a range of 1 GW to 2.4 GW. A small modular reactor (SMR), of 250 MW, would come online by mid-century, the NECP reads. Slovenia plans to maintain a high level of electricity connectivity with neighboring countries, with a goal of more than 80%. At least 85% of power supply needs to be from domestic sources in 2030 and 100% by 2040, the government said. Another target for the current decade is to cover at least 75% of electricity demand in the transmission network, during peak load hours, with domestic production. After 2033 the level is 80%. According to the European Commission, one third of member states are still due to submit their final updates. They include Bulgaria, Croatia and Greece, but the Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan webpage could itself need an update. A key issue is the weak renewable energy target, falling over 10% below the EU Commission’s recommendation. GHG emission reduction targets remain unchanged from the 2023 version, while final and primary energy reduction targets have improved but still fall short of Paris Agreement requirements. Another major issue is the substantial weakening of fossil fuel subsidy phase-out measures and targets compared to the 2023 draft and the currently valid 2019 NECP.   Click HERE to download the Slovenian draft NECP country assessment Slovenia – climate action progress in figures Check Slovenia’s implementation of its National Energy and Climate Plan Slovenia’s draft NECP update falls short of aligning with a 1.5°C target, lacking concrete measures or policies. Moreover, as of 2022, Slovenia was not fully on track to implement its old 2019 NECP, whose ambition is now obsolete. While both gross and net emissions were on a declining trend, emissions from the LULUCF sector raise concerns: values have worsened every year since 2019. Slovenia is also off the decarbonisation trajectory projected in the 2019 NECP for non-ETS sectors, with 2022 values surpassing pre-pandemic levels (11.1 MtCO2-eq compared to 10.8 in 2019). The available data indicates that the transport sector is an important component of this surge in emissions. As of 2022, Slovenia was on track to implement the 2030 objectives set for energy efficiency in the old 2019 NECP tracker (nonetheless, increased efforts will be needed to achieve the new 2030 targets). On the other hand, Slovenia is slightly below expectations of the 2019 NECP when it comes to the share of renewables in final energy consumption.
